# [Monday 30 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/30/)

Up before day, and by coach to Westminster, and there first to [Sir H. Cholmly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5179/), and there I did to my great content deliver him up his little several papers for sums of money paid him, and took his regular receipts upon his orders, wherein I am safe. Thence to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there to visit [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/), and there was with him a great while, and [my Lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4039/) and they seem in very good humour, but by and by Sir G. Carteret and I alone, and there we did talk of the ruinous condition we are in, [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) being going to put out of the Council so many able men; such as my [Lord Anglesey](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/887/), [Ashly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/215/), [Hollis](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/886/), [Secretary Morrice](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5947/) (to bring in [Mr. Trevor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11972/)), and the [Archbishop of Canterbury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2519/), and my [Lord Bridgewater](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11086/). He tells me that this is true, only the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) do endeavour to hinder it, and the Duke of York himself did tell him so: that the King and the Duke of York do not in company disagree, but are friendly; but that there is a core in their hearts, he doubts, which is not to be easily removed; for these men do suffer only for their constancy to the [Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/), or at least from the King’s ill-will against him: that they do now all they can to vilify the clergy, and do accuse [Rochester](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10263/) [Dolben] … [of his being given to boys and of his putting his hand into a gentleman (who now comes to bear evidence against him) his codpiece while they were at table together. – L&M] And so do raise scandals, all that is possible, against other of the Bishops. He do suggest that something is intended for the [Duke of Monmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5315/), and it may be, against [the Queene](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) also: that we are in no manner sure against an invasion the next year: that the [Duke of Buckingham](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2558/) do rule all now, and the Duke of York comes indeed to [the Caball](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13278/), but signifies little there. That this new faction do not endure, nor the King, [Sir W. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/); but yet that he is so usefull that they cannot be without him; but that he is not now called to the Caball. That my Lord of Buckingham, [Bristoll](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2845/), and [Arlington](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5520/), do seem to agree in these things; but that they do not in their hearts trust one another, but do drive several ways, all of them. In short, he do bless himself that he is no more concerned in matters now; and the hopes he hath of being at liberty, when his accounts are over, to retire into the country. That he do give over the kingdom for wholly lost. So after some other little discourse, I away, meeting with [Mr. Cooling](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1027/). I with him by coach to [the Wardrobe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/946/), where I never was since [the fire](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10319/) in [Hatton Garden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10948/), but did not ’light: and he tells me he fears that my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) will suffer much by [Mr. Townsend’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/947/) being untrue to him, he being now unable to give the [Commissioners of the Treasury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11226/) an account of his money received by many thousands of pounds, which I am troubled for.

Thence to the [Old Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/) together, he telling me that he believes there will be no such turning out of great men as is talked of, but that it is only to fright people, but I do fear there may be such a thing doing. He do mightily inveigh against the folly of the King to bring his matters to wrack thus, and that we must all be undone without help. I met with Cooling at the [Temple-gate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/503/), after I had been at both [my](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11024/)[booksellers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11465/) and there laid out several pounds in books now against the new year. From the ’Change (where I met with [Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), who would have borrowed money of me, but I had the grace to deny him, he would have had 3 or 400 _l._) I with Cocke and [Mr. Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9022/) (whose wife was just now brought to bed of a boy, but he seems not to be at all taken with it, which is a strange consideration how others do rejoice to have a child born), to Sir G. Carteret’s, in [Lincoln’s Inn Fields](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/125/), and there did dine together, there being there, among other company, [Mr. Attorney Montagu](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/563/), and [his fine lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3690/), a fine woman. After dinner, I did understand from my [Lady Jemimah](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/114/) that her brother [Hinchingbroke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/113/) business was to be ended this day, as she thinks, towards his match, and they do talk here of their intent to buy themselves some new clothes against the wedding, which I am very glad of. After dinner I did even with Sir G. Carteret the accounts of the interest of the money which I did so long put out for him in [Sir R. Viner’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8584/) hands, and by it I think I shall be a gainer about 28 _l._, which is a very good reward for the little trouble I have had in it. Thence with [Sir Philip Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8250/) to the [King’s playhouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/475/), there to see [“Love’s Cruelty,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11973/) an old play, but which I have not seen before; and in the first act [Orange Moll](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10310/) come to me, with one of our porters by my house, to tell me that [Mrs. Pierce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/785/) and [Knepp](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9483/) did dine at my house to-day, and that I was desired to come [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/). So I went out presently, and by coach home, and they were just gone away so, after a very little stay with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), I took coach again, and to the King’s playhouse again, and come in the fourth act; and it proves to me a very silly play, and to everybody else, as far as I could judge. But the jest is, that here telling Moll how I had lost my journey, she told me that Mrs. Knepp was in the house, and so shews me to her, and I went to her, and sat out the play, and then with her to [Mrs. Manuel’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11497/), where Mrs. Pierce was, and her [boy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9472/) and [girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9044/); and here I did hear Mrs. Manuel and one of the Italians, her gallant, sing well. But yet I confess I am not delighted so much with it, as to admire it: for, not understanding the words, I lose the benefit of the vocalitys of the musick, and it proves only instrumental; and therefore was more pleased to hear Knepp sing two or three little English things that I understood, though the composition of the other, and performance, was very fine. Thence, after sitting and talking a pretty while, I took leave and left them there, and so to my bookseller’s, and paid for the books I had bought, and away home, where I told my wife where I had been. But she was as mad as a devil, and nothing but ill words between us all the evening while we sat at [cards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/797/) — [W. Hewer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/) and [the girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/) by — even to gross ill words, which I was troubled for, but do see that I must use policy to keep her spirit down, and to give her no offence by my being with Knepp and Pierce, of which, though she will not own it, yet she is heartily jealous. At last it ended in few words and my silence (which for fear of growing higher between us I did forbear), and so to supper and to bed without one word one to another.

This day I did carry money out, and paid several debts. Among others, [my tailor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9587/), and shoemaker, and draper, [Sir W. Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3725/), who begun to talk of the [Commission of accounts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/12029/), wherein he is one; but though they are the greatest people that ever were in the nation as to power, and like to be our judges, yet I did never speak one word to him of desiring favour, or bidding him joy in it, but did answer him to what he said, and do resolve to stand or fall by my silent preparing to answer whatever can be laid to me, and that will be my best proceeding, I think. This day I got a little rent in my new fine [camlett](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11928/) cloak with the latch of Sir G. Carteret’s door; but it is darned up at my tailor’s, that it will be no great blemish to it; but it troubled me. I could not but observe that Sir Philip Carteret would fain have given me my going into a play; but yet, when he come to the door, he had no money to pay for himself, I having refused to accept of it for myself, but was fain; and I perceive he is known there, and do run upon the score for plays, which is a shame; but I perceive always he is in want of money.1

In the pit I met with [Sir Ch. North](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/725/), formerly Mr. North, who was with my Lord at sea; and he, of his own accord, was so silly as to tell me he [is married](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11974/); and for her quality (being a Lord’s daughter, my Lord Grey), and person, and beauty, and years, and estate, and disposition, he is the happiest man in the world. I am sure he is an ugly fellow; but a good scholar and sober gentleman; and heir to his father, now [Lord North](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/726/), the [old Lord](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14142/) being dead.

>

# [Tuesday 31 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/31/)

Up, without words to [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), or few, and those not angry, and so to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there waited a long time, while the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) was with [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) in [the Caball](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13278/), and there I and [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/) stayed talking without, in the [Vane-Room](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7036/), and I perceive all people’s expectation is, what will be the issue of this great business of putting these great Lords out of the council and power, the quarrel, I perceive, being only their standing against the will of the King in the business of [the Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/). Anon the Duke of York comes out, and then to a [committee of Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5243/), where my [Lord Middleton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7228/) did come to-day, and seems to me but a dull, heavy man; but he is a great soldier, and stout, and a needy Lord, which will still keep that poor garrison from ever coming to be worth anything to the King. Here, after a short meeting, we broke up, and I home to the office, where they are sitting, and so I to them, and having done our business rose, and I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner with my people, and there dined with me my uncle [Thomas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2542/), with a mourning hat-band on, for his daughter [Mary](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2934/), and here I and my people did discourse of the [Act for the accounts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/12029/), which do give the greatest power to these people, as they report that have read it (I having not yet read it, and indeed its nature is such as I have no mind to go about to read it, for fear of meeting matter in it to trouble me), that ever was given to any subjects, and too much also. After dinner with my wife and [girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/) to [Unthanke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1201/), and there left her, and I to Westminster, and there to [Mrs. Martin’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1157/), and did hazer con elle what I desired, and there did drink with her, and find fault with [her husband’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7729/) wearing of too fine clothes, by which I perceive he will be a beggar, and so after a little talking I away and took up my wife again, and so home and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where [Captain Perryman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10970/) did give me an account, walking in the garden, how the seamen of England are discouraged by want of money (or otherwise by being, as he says, but I think without cause, by their being underrated) so far as that he thinks the greatest part are gone abroad or going, and says that it is known that there are Irish in the town, up and down, that do labour to entice the seamen out of the nation by giving them 3 _l._ in hand, and promise of 40 _s._ per month, to go into the [King of France’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5855/) service, which is a mighty shame, but yet I believe is true. I did advise with him about my little vessel, [“The Maybolt,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11665/) which he says will be best for me to sell, though my employing her to [Newcastle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7005/) this winter, and the next spring, for coles, will be a gainful trade, but yet make me great trouble, but I will think of it, and so to my office, ended my letters, and so home to supper and to bed, good friends with my wife.

Thus ends the year, with great happiness to myself and family as to health and good condition in the world, blessed be God for it! only with great trouble to my mind in reference to the publick, there being little hopes left but that the whole nation must in a very little time be lost, either by troubles at home, the [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) being dissatisfied, and the King led into unsettled councils by some about him, himself considering little, and divisions growing between the King and Duke of York; or else by foreign invasion, to which we must submit if any, at this bad point of time, should come upon us, which the King of France is well able to do. These thoughts, and some cares upon me, concerning my standing in this Office when the Committee of Parliament shall come to examine our Navy matters, which they will now shortly do. I pray God they may do the kingdom service therein, as they will have sufficient opportunity of doing it!

# Diary entries from December 1663

# [Tuesday 1 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/01/)

Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning. At noon I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner with my poor [wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), with whom now-a-days I enjoy great pleasure in her company and learning of [Arithmetique](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/370/).

After dinner I to [Guild Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/129/) to hear a tryall at [King’s Bench](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14046/), before [Lord Chief Justice Hide](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7025/), about the insurance of a ship, the same I mention in my [yesterday’s journall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/11/30/), where everything was proved how money was so taken up upon [bottomary](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1590/) and insurance, and the ship left by the master and seamen upon rocks, where, when the sea fell at the ebb, she must perish. The master was offered helpe, and he did give the pilotts 20 sols to drink to bid them go about their business, saying that the rocks were old, but his ship was new, and that she was repaired for 6 _l._ and less all the damage that she received, and is now brought by one, sent for on purpose by the insurers, into [the Thames](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1832/), with her cargo, vessels of tallow daubed over with [butter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5148/), instead of all butter, the whole not worth above 500 _l._, ship and all, and they had took up, as appeared, above 2,400 _l._. He had given his men money to content them; and yet, for all this, he did bring some of them to swear that it was very stormy weather, and [they] did all they could to save her, and that she was seven feete deep water in hold, and were fain to cut her main and foremast, that the master was the last man that went out, and they were fain to force [him] out when she was ready to sink; and her rudder broke off, and she was drawn into the harbour after they were gone, as wrecke all broken, and goods lost: that she could not be carried out again without new building, and many other things so contrary as is not imaginable more. There was all the great counsel in the kingdom in the cause; but after one witnesse or two for the plaintiff, it was cried down as a most notorious cheate; and so the jury, without going out, found it for the plaintiff. But it was pleasant to see what mad sort of testimonys the seamen did give, and could not be got to speak in order: and then their terms such as the judge could not understand; and to hear how sillily the Counsel and judge would speak as to the terms necessary in the matter, would make one laugh: and above all, a Frenchman that was forced to speak in French, and took an English oathe he did not understand, and had an interpreter sworn to tell us what he said, which was the best testimony of all. So home well satisfied with this afternoon’s work, purposing to spend an afternoon or two every [term](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14059/) so, and so to my office a while and then home to supper, arithmetique with my wife, and to bed.

I heard other causes, and saw the course of pleading by being at this trial, and heard and learnt two things: one is that every man has a right of passage in, but not a title to, any highway. The next, that the judge would not suffer [Mr. Crow](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1475/), who hath fined for Alderman, to be called so, but only Mister, and did eight or nine times fret at it, and stop every man that called him so.

# [Wednesday 2 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/02/)

[My wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) troubled all last night with the toothache and this morning.

I up and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where busy, and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner with my wife, who is better of her tooth than she was, and in the afternoon by agreement called on by [Mr. Bland](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5181/), and with him to [the Ship](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7026/) a neighbour tavern and there met his antagonist [Mr. Custos](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7027/) and his referee [Mr. Clarke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6856/) a merchant also, and begun the dispute about the freight of a ship hired by Mr. Bland to carry provisions to [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/), and the freight is now demanded, whereas he says that the goods were some spoiled, some not delivered, and upon the whole demands 1300 _l._ of the other, and their minds are both so high, their demands so distant, and their words so many and hot against one another that I fear we shall bring it to nothing. But however I am glad to see myself so capable of understanding the business as I find I do, and shall endeavour to do Mr. Bland all the just service I can therein.

Here we were in a bad room, which vexed me most, but we meet at another house next. So at noon I home and to my office till 9 o’clock, and so home to my wife to keep her company, [arithmetique](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/370/), then to supper, and to bed, she being well of her tooth again.

# [Thursday 3 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/03/)

Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where all the forenoon, and then (by [Mr. Coventry’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) coach) to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, very pleasant with [my poor wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/). Somebody from [Portsmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1764/), I know not who, has this day sent me a Runlett of [Tent](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/). So to my office all the afternoon, where much business till late at night, and so home to my wife, and then to supper and to bed.

This day [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) did tell us at the table, that the Navy (excepting what is due to the Yards upon the quarter now going on, and what few bills he hath not heard of) is quite out of debt; which is extraordinary good newes, and upon the ’Change to hear how our creditt goes as good as any merchant’s upon the ’Change is a joyfull thing to consider, which God continue! I am sure [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) will have the benefit of it, as well as we some peace and creditt.

# [Friday 4 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/04/)

Up pretty betimes, that is about 7 o’clock, it being now dark then, and so got me ready, with my clothes, breeches and warm [stockings](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/516/), and by water with [Henry Russell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6482/), cold and wet and windy to [Woolwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1675/), to a [hempe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5171/) ship there, and staid looking upon it and giving direction as to the getting it ashore, and so back again very cold, and at home without going on shore anywhere about 12 o’clock, being fearful of taking cold, and so dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) and shifted myself, and so all the afternoon at [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) till night, and then home to keep [my poor wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) company, and so to supper and to bed.

# [Saturday 5 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/05/)

Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning, and then with the whole board, viz., [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/), [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/), and myself along with [Captain Allen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1330/) home to dinner, where he lives hard by in [Mark Lane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3333/), where we had a very good plain dinner and good welcome, in a pretty little house but so smoky that it was troublesome to us all till they put out the fire, and made one of charcoale.

I was much pleased with this dinner for the many excellent stories told by [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/), which I have put down in my book of tales and so shall not mention them here.

We staid till night, and then Mr. Coventry away, and by and by I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to my office till 9 or 10 at night, and so home to supper and to bed after some talke and [Arithmetique](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/370/) with [my poor wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), with whom now-a-days I live with great content, out of all trouble of mind by jealousy (for which God forgive me), or any other distraction more than my fear of my [Lord Sandwich’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) displeasure.

# [Sunday 6 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/06/)

(Lord’s day). Lay long in bed, and then up and to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/) alone, which is the greatest trouble that I have by not having a man or, boy to wait on me, and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), it being a cold day, and it begun to snow (the first snow we have seen this year) kept her bed till after dinner, and I below by myself looking over my [arithmetique](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/370/) books and [timber rule](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6104/).

So my wife rose anon, and she and I all the afternoon at arithmetique, and she is come to do Addition, Subtraction, and Multiplicacion very well, and so I purpose not to trouble her yet with Division, but to begin with the [Globes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6732/) to her now.

At night came [Captain Grove](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5952/) to discourse with me about [Field’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3815/) business and of other matters, and so, he being gone, I to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and spent an houre or two reading [Rushworth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7002/), and so to supper home, and to prayers and bed, finding myself by cold to have some pain begin with me, which God defend should increase.

# [Monday 7 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/07/)

Up betimes, and, it being a frosty morning, walked on foot to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), but not without some fear of my pain coming. At White Hall I hear and find that there was the last night the greatest tide that ever was remembered in England to have been in this river: all White Hall having been drowned, of which there was great discourse.

Anon we all met, and up with [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) and did our business, and by and by my [Lord of Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) came in, but whether it be my doubt or no I cannot tell, but I do not find that he made any sign of kindnesse or respect to me, which troubles me more than any thing in the world. After done there [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) and [Captain Allen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1330/) and I by coach to [the Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/131/), where I ’light, they going home, and indeed it being my trouble of mind to try whether I could meet with my Lord Sandwich and try him to see how he will receive me. I took coach and back again to Whitehall, but there could not find him. But here I met [Dr. Clerke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/770/), and did tell him my story of my health; how my pain comes to me now-a-days. He did write something for me which I shall take when there is occasion. I then fell to other discourse of [Dr. Knapp](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7035/), who tells me he is [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) physician, and is become a solicitor for places for people, and I am mightily troubled with him. He tells me he is the most impudent fellow in the world, that gives himself out to be the King’s physician, but it is not so, but is cast out of the Court. From thence I may learn what impudence there is in the world, and how a man may be deceived in persons.

Anon the King and Duke and [Duchesse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1402/) came to dinner in [the Vane-roome](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7036/), where I never saw them before; but it seems since the tables are done, he dines there all together.

[The Queene](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) is pretty well, and goes out of her chamber to her little chappell in the house. [The King of France](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5855/), they say, is hiring of sixty sail of ships of the Dutch, but it is not said for what design.

By and by, not hoping to see my Lord, I went to the [King’s Head](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1110/)[ordinary](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1199/), where a good dinner but no discourse almost, and after dinner by coach, [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and found [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) this cold day not yet out of bed, and after a little good talk with her to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and there spent my time till late.

[Sir W. Warren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/) two or three hours with me talking of trade, and other very good discourse, which did please me very, well, and so, after reading in [Rushworth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7002/), home to supper and to bed.

# [Tuesday 8 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/08/)

Lay long in bed, and then up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning, and among other things my [Lord Barkely](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1055/) called in question his clerk [Mr. Davy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1528/) for something which [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) and I did tell him yesterday, but I endeavoured to make the least of it, and so all was put up.

At noon to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and among other businesses did discourse with [Captain Taylor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2214/), and I think I shall safely get 20 _l._ by his ship’s freight at present, besides what it may be I may get hereafter.

So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and thence by coach to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), where a great while walked with my [Lord Tiviott](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5727/), whom I find a most carefull, thoughtfull, and cunning man, as I also ever took him to be. He is this day bringing in an account where he makes [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) debtor to him 10,000 _l._ already on the garrison of [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) account; but yet demands not ready money to pay it, but offers such ways of paying it out of the sale of old decayed provisions as will enrich him finely.

Anon came my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), and then we fell to our business at [the Committee](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5243/) about my Lord Tiviott’s accounts, wherein I took occasion to speak now and then, so as my Lord Sandwich did well seem to like of it, and after we were up did bid me good night in a tone that, methinks, he is not so displeased with me as I did doubt he is; however, I will take a course to know whether he be or no.

The Committee done, I took coach and home to my office, and there late, and so to supper at home, and to bed, being doubtful of my pain through the very cold weather which we have, but I will take all the care I can to prevent it.

# [Wednesday 9 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/09/)

Lay very long in bed for fear of my pain, and then rose and went to stool (after [my wife’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) way, who by all means would have me sit long and upright) very well, and being ready to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/). From thence I was called by and by to my wife, she not being well. So to her, and found her in great pain … [of those. – L&M] So by and by to my office again, and then abroad to look out a cradle to burn charcoal in at my office, and I found one to my mind in [Newgate Market](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5730/), and so meeting [Hoby’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5669/) man in the street, I spoke to him to serve it in to the office for [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/). So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and after talk with my wife, she in bed and pain all day, I to my office most of the evening, and then home to my wife. This day [Mrs. Russell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6632/) did give my wife a very fine St. George, in alabaster, which will set out my wife’s closett mightily.

This evening at the office, after I had wrote my day’s passages, there came to me my cozen [Angier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2804/) of Cambridge, poor man, making his moan, and obtained of me that I would send [his son](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6367/) to sea as a [Reformado](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/674/), which I will take care to do. But to see how apt every man is to forget friendship in time of adversity. How glad was I when he was gone, for fear he should ask me to be bond for him, or to borrow money of me.

# [Thursday 10 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/10/)

Up, pretty well, the weather being become pretty warm again, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning, and I confess having received so lately a token from [Mrs. Russell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6632/), I did find myself concerned for our not buying some tallow of her (which she bought on purpose yesterday most unadvisedly to her great losse upon confidence of putting it off to us). So hard it is for a man not to be warped against his duty and master’s interest that receives any bribe or present, though not as a bribe, from any body else. But she must be contented, and I to do her a good turn when I can without wrong to [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) service.

Then [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner (and did drink a glass of [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/) and [beer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/308/), the more for joy that this is the shortest day in the year, —[Old Style]— which is a pleasant consideration) with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/). She in bed but pretty well, and having a messenger from [my brother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/236/), that he is not well nor stirs out of doors, I went forth to see him, and found him below, he has not been well, but is not ill. I found him taking order for the distribution of [Mrs. Ramsey’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2841/) coals, a thing [my father](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/154/) for many years did, and now he after him, which I was glad to see, as also to hear that [Mr. Wheatly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2974/) begins to look after him. I hope it is about his daughter.

Thence to [St. Paul’s Church Yard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/182/), to [my bookseller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1539/), and having gained this day in the office by my stationer’s bill to the King about 40 _s._ or 3 _l._, I did here sit two or three hours calling for twenty books to lay this money out upon, and found myself at a great losse where to choose, and do see how my nature would gladly return to laying out money in this trade. I could not tell whether to lay out my money for books of pleasure, as plays, which my nature was most earnest in; but at last, after seeing Chaucer, [Dugdale’s History of Paul’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7037/), [Stows London](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7038/), [Gesner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7039/), History of Trent, besides Shakespeare, [Jonson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7040/), and [Beaumont’s plays](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7041/), I at last chose [Dr. Fuller’s Worthys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1841/), [the Cabbala or Collections of Letters of State](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7042/), and a little book, [Delices de Hollande](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7043/), with another little book or two, all of good use or serious pleasure: and [Hudibras](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5746/), both parts, the book now in greatest fashion for drollery, though I cannot, I confess, see enough where the wit lies. My mind being thus settled, I went by [linke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1167/) home, and so to my office, and to read in [Rushworth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7002/); and so home to supper and to bed.

Calling at [Wotton’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/564/), my shoemaker’s, today, he tells me that [Sir H. Wright](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/550/) is dying; and that [Harris](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6533/) is come to [the Duke’s house](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2935/) again; and of a rare play to be acted this week of [Sir William Davenant’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/992/): [the story of Henry the Eighth with all his wives](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7044/).

# [Friday 11 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/11/)

Up and abroad toward [the Wardrobe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/946/), and going out [Mr. Clerke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5255/) met me to tell me that [Field](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3815/) has a writ against me in this last business of 30 _l._ 10 _s._, and that he believes he will get an execution against me this morning, and though he told me it could not be well before noon, and that he would stop it at the [Sheriff’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11773/), yet it is hard to believe with what fear I did walk and how I did doubt at every man I saw and do start at the hearing of one man cough behind my neck. I to the Wardrobe and there missed [Mr. Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/340/). So to [Mr. Holden’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2187/) and evened all reckonings there for hats, and then walked to [Paul’s Churchyard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/182/) and after a little at [my bookseller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1539/) and bought at a shop [Cardinall Mazarin’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2311/)[Will in French](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7045/). I to the [Coffeehouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/813/) and there among others had good discourse with an Iron Merchant, who tells me the great evil of discouraging our natural manufacture of England in that commodity by suffering the Swede to bring in three times more than ever they did and our owne Ironworks be lost, as almost half of them, he says, are already. Then I went and sat by [Mr. Harrington](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7046/), and some East country merchants, and talking of the country about [Quinsborough](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7053/), and thereabouts, he told us himself that for fish, none there, the poorest body, will buy a dead fish, but must be alive, unless it be in winter; and then they told us the manner of putting their nets into the water. Through holes made in the thick ice, they will spread a net of half a mile long; and he hath known a hundred and thirty and a hundred and seventy barrels of fish taken at one draught. And then the people come with sledges upon the ice, with snow at the bottome, and lay the fish in and cover them with snow, and so carry them to market. And he hath seen when the said fish have been frozen in the sledge, so as that he hath taken a fish and broke a-pieces, so hard it hath been; and yet the same fishes taken out of the snow, and brought into a hot room, will be alive and leap up and down. Swallows are often brought up in their nets out of the mudd from under water, hanging together to some twigg or other, dead in ropes, and brought to the fire will come to life. Fowl killed in December ([Alderman Barker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5175/) said) he did buy, and putting into the box under his sledge, did forget to take them out to eate till Aprill next, and they then were found there, and were through the frost as sweet and fresh and eat as well as at first killed. Young beares are there; their flesh sold in market as ordinarily as beef here, and is excellent sweet meat. They tell us that beares there do never hurt any body, but fly away from you, unless you pursue and set upon them; but wolves do much mischief. Mr. Harrington told us how they do to get so much [honey](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6861/) as they send abroad. They make hollow a great fir-tree, leaving only a small slitt down straight in one place, and this they close up again, only leave a little hole, and there the [bees](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13820/) go in and fill the bodys of those trees as full of wax and honey as they can hold; and the inhabitants at times go and open the slit, and take what they please without killing the bees, and so let them live there still and make more. Fir trees are always planted close together, because of keeping one another from the violence of the windes; and when a fell is made, they leave here and there a grown tree to preserve the young ones coming up. The great entertainment and sport of the [Duke of Corland](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7067/), and the princes thereabouts, is hunting; which is not with dogs as we, but he appoints such a day, and summons all the country-people as to a campagnia; and by several companies gives every one their circuit, and they agree upon a place where the toyle is to be set; and so making fires every company as they go, they drive all the wild beasts, whether bears, wolves, foxes, swine, and stags, and roes, into the toyle; and there the great men have their stands in such and such places, and shoot at what they have a mind to, and that is their hunting. They are not very populous there, by reason that people marry women seldom till they are towards or above thirty; and men thirty or forty years old, or more oftentimes.

Against a publique hunting the Duke sends that no wolves be killed by the people; and whatever harm they do, the Duke makes it good to the person that suffers it: as Mr. Harrington instanced in a house where he lodged, where a wolfe broke into a hog-stye, and bit three or four great pieces off the back of the hog, before the house could come to helpe it (it calling, and that did give notice to the people of the house); and the man of the house told him that there were three or four wolves thereabouts that did them great hurt; but it was no matter, for the Duke was to make it good to him, otherwise he would kill them.

Hence [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) and upstairs, [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) keeping her bed, and had a very good dinner, and after dinner to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and there till late busy. Among other things [Captain Taylor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2214/) came to me about his bill for freight, and besides that I found him contented that I have the 30 _l._ I got, he do offer me to give me 6 _l._ to take the getting of the bill paid upon me, which I am ready to do, but I am loath to have it said that I ever did it. However, I will do him the service to get it paid if I can and stand to his courtesy what he will give me.

Late to supper home, and to my great joy I have by my wife’s good advice almost brought myself by going often and leisurely to the stool that I am come almost to have my natural course of stool as well as ever, which I pray God continue to me.

# [Saturday 12 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/12/)

Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) where all the morning, and among other things got [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) to put his letters to [Captain Taylor’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2214/) bill by which I am in hopes to get 5 _l._, which joys my heart. We had this morning a great dispute between [Mr. Gauden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/994/), Victualler of the Navy, and [Sir J. Lawson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/110/), and the rest of the Commanders going against [Argier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3088/), about their fish and keeping of [Lent](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/469/); which Mr. Gauden so much insists upon to have it observed, as being the only thing that makes up the loss of his dear bargain all the rest of the year.

At noon went home and there I found that one [Abrahall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7055/), who strikes in for the serving of [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) with Ship chandlery ware, has sent [my wif](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/)e a Japan gowne, which pleases her very well and me also, it coming very opportune, but I know not how to carry myself to him, I being already obliged so far to [Mrs. Russell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6632/), so that I am in both their pays.

To [the Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), where I had sent [Luellin](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/506/) word I would come to him, and thence brought him home to dinner with me. He tells me that [W. Symon’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/916/)[wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/924/) is dead, for which I am sorry, she being a good woman, and tells me an odde story of her saying before her death, being in good sense, that there stood her uncle [Scobell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1231/).

Then he began to tell me that [Mr. Deering](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7073/) had been with him to desire him to speak to me that if I would get him off with these goods upon his hands, he would give me 50 pieces, and further that if I would stand his friend to helpe him to the benefit of his patent as the King’s merchant, he could spare me 200 _l._ per annum out of his profits. I was glad to hear both of these, but answered him no further than that as I would not by any thing be bribed to be unjust in my dealings,1 so I was not so squeamish as not to take people’s acknowledgment where I had the good fortune by my pains to do them good and just offices, and so I would not come to be at any agreement with him, but I would labour to do him this service and to expect his consideration thereof afterwards as he thought fit. So I expect to hear more of it.

I did make very much of Luellin in hopes to have some good by this business, and in the evening received some money from [Mr. Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/340/), and so went and settled accounts in my books between him and me, and I do hope at [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/) not only to find myself as rich or more than ever I was yet, but also my accounts in less compass, fewer reckonings either of debts or moneys due to me, than ever I have been for some years, and indeed do so, the goodness of God bringing me from better to a better expectation and hopes of doing well. This day I heard my [Lord Barkeley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1055/) tell [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) that he hath letters from France that the King hath unduked twelve Dukes, only to show his power and to crush his nobility, who he said he did see had heretofore laboured to cross him. And this my Lord Barkeley did mightily magnify, as a sign of a brave and vigorous mind, that what he saw fit to be done he dares do.

At night, after business done at my office, [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to supper and to bed.

I have forgot to set down a very remarkable passage that, Lewellen being gone, and I going into the office, and it begun to be dark, I found nobody there, my clerks being at the burial of a child of [W. Griffin’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1529/), and so I spent a little time till they came, walking in the garden, and in the mean time, while I was walking [Mrs. Pen’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2849/) pretty maid came by my side, and went into the office, but finding nobody there I went in to her, being glad of the occasion. She told me as she was going out again that there was nobody there, and that she came for a sheet of paper. So I told her I would supply her, and left her in the office and went into my office and opened my garden door, thinking to have got her in, and there to have caressed her, and seeming looking for paper, I told her this way was as near a way for her, but she told me she had left the door open and so did not come to me. So I carried her some paper and kissed her, leading her by the hand to the garden door and there let her go. But, Lord! to see how much I was put out of order by this surprisal, and how much I could have subjected my mind to have treated and been found with this wench, and how afterwards I was troubled to think what if she should tell this and whether I had spoke or done any thing that might be unfit for her to tell. But I think there was nothing more passed than just what I here write.

1.   Edward Dering was granted, August, 1660, “the office of King’s merchant in the East, for buying and providing necessaries for apparelling the Navy” (“Calendar,” Domestic, 1660-61, p. 212). There is evidence among the State Papers of some dissatisfaction with the timber, &c., which he supplied to the Navy, and at this time he appears to have had some stores left on his hands. ↩

# [Sunday 13 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/13/)

(Lord’s day). Up and made me ready for Church, but [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I had a difference about her old folly that she would fasten lies upon her mayds, and now upon [Jane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6655/), which I did not see enough to confirm me in it, and so would not consent to her.

To [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), where after sermon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), before dinner, reading my vowes, and so home to dinner, where [Tom](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/236/) came to me and he and I dined together, [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) not rising all day, and after dinner I made even accounts with him, and spent all the afternoon in my chamber talking of many things with him, and about [Wheately’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2974/) daughter for a wife for him, and then about [the](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1107/)[Joyces](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1090/) and their father [Fenner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/749/), how they are sometimes all honey one with another and then all turd, and a strange rude life there is among them.

In the evening, he gone, I to my office to read [Rushworth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7002/) upon the charge and answer of the [Duke of Buckingham](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/857/), which is very fine, and then to do a little business against to-morrow, and so home to supper to my wife, and then to bed.

# [Monday 14 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/14/)

Up by candlelight, which I do not use to do, though it be very late, that is to say almost 8 o’clock, and out by coach to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), where we all met and to [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/), where I heard a large discourse between one that goes over an agent from [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) to [Legorne](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7069/) and thereabouts, to remove the inconveniences his ships are put to by denial of [pratique](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7070/); which is a thing that is now-a-days made use of only as a cheat, for a man may buy a bill of health for a [piece of eight](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6260/), and my enemy may agree with the Intendent of the Sante for ten pieces of eight or so; that he shall not give me a bill of health, and so spoil me in my design, whatever it be. This the King will not endure, and so resolves either to have it removed, or to keep all ships from coming in, or going out there, so long as his ships are stayed for want hereof.

Then, my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) being there, we all went into the Duke’s closet and did our business. But among other things, Lord! what an account did [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) and [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) make of the pulling down and burning of the head of [the Charles](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/462/), where [Cromwell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/796/) was placed with people under his horse, and Peter, as the Duke called him, is praying to him; and Sir J. Minnes would needs infer the temper of the people from their joy at the doing of this and their building a gibbet for the hanging of his head up, when God knows, it is even the flinging away of 100 _l._ out of the King’s purse, to the building of another, which it seems must be a Neptune.

Thence I through White Hall only to see what was doing, but meeting none that I knew I went through the garden to my Lord Sandwich’s lodging, where I found my Lord got before me (which I did not intend or expect) and was there trying some musique, which he intends for an anthem of three parts, I know not whether for the King’s chapel or no, but he seems mighty intent upon it. But it did trouble me to hear him swear before God and other oathes, as he did now and then without any occasion, which methinks did so ill become him, and I hope will be a caution for me, it being so ill a thing in him.

The musique being done, without showing me any good or ill countenance, he did give me his hat and so adieu, and went down to his coach without saying anything to me. He being gone I and [Mr. Howe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/549/) talked a good while. He tells me that my Lord, it is true, for a while after my letter, was displeased, and did shew many slightings of me when he had occasion of mentioning me to his Lordship, but that now my Lord is in good temper and he do believe will shew me as much respect as ever, and would have me not to refrain to come to him. This news I confess did much trouble me, but when I did hear how he is come to himself, and hath wholly left [Chelsy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2610/), and the slut, and that I see he do follow his business, and becomes in better repute than before, I am rejoiced to see it, though it do cost me some disfavour for a time, for if not his good nature and ingenuity, yet I believe his memory will not bear it always in his mind. But it is my comfort that this is the thing that after so many years good service that has made him my enemy.

Thence to the [King’s Head](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1110/) ordinary, and there dined among a company of fine gentlemen; some of them discoursed of the [King of France’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5855/) greatness, and how he is come to make the Princes of the Blood to take place of all foreign Embassadors, which it seems is granted by them of [Venice](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13485/) and other States, and expected from my [Lord. Hollis](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/886/), our King’s Embassador there; and that either upon that score or something else he hath not had his entry yet in [Paris](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8787/), but hath received several affronts, and among others his harnesse cut, and his gentlemen of his horse killed, which will breed bad blood if true. They say also that the King of France hath hired threescore ships of Holland, and forty of the Swede, but nobody knows what to do; but some great designs he hath on foot against the next year.

Thence by coach home and to my office, where I spent all the evening till night with [Captain Taylor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2214/) discoursing about keeping of [masts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5619/), and when he was gone, with [Sir W. Warren,](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/) who did give me excellent discourse about the same thing, which I have committed to paper, and then fell to other talk of his being at [Chatham](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/643/) lately and there discoursing of his masts. [Commissioner Pett](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/708/) did let fall several scurvy words concerning my pretending to know masts as well as any body, which I know proceeds ever since I told him I could measure a piece of [timber](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5172/) as well as anybody employed by the King. But, however, I shall remember him for a black sheep again a good while, with all his fair words to me, and perhaps may let him know that my ignorance does the King as much good as all his knowledge, which would do more it is true if it were well used.

Then we fell to talk of Sir J. Minnes’s and Sir W. Batten’s burning of Oliver’s head, while he was there; which was done with so much insulting and folly as I never heard of, and had the [Trayned Band](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1782/) of [Rochester](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/894/) to come to the solemnity, which when all comes to all, Commissioner Pett says it never was made for him; but it troubles me the King should suffer 100 _l._ losse in his purse, to make a new one after it was forgot whose it was, or any words spoke of it.

He being gone I mightily pleased with his discourse, by which I always learn something, I to read a little in [Rushworth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7002/), and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to supper to [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), it having been washing day, and so to bed, my mind I confess a little troubled for my Lord Sandwich’s displeasure. But God will give me patience to bear since it rises from so good an occasion.

# [Tuesday 15 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/15/)

Before I was up, [my brother’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/236/) man came to tell me that my cozen, [Edward Pepys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/342/), was dead, died at [Mrs. Turner’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/121/), for which [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I are very sorry, and the more for that [his wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2531/) was the only handsome woman of our name.

So up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where the greatest business was [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) and [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) against me for [Sir W. Warren’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/) contract for [masts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5619/), to which I may go to my memorandum book to see what past, but came off with conquest, and my [Lord Barkely](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1055/) and [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) well convinced that we are well used.

So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and thither came to me [Mr. Mount](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/571/) and [Mr. Luellin](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/506/), I think almost foxed, and there dined with me and very merry as I could be, my mind being troubled to see things so ordered at the Board, though with no disparagement to me at all.

At dinner comes a messenger from [the Counter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7071/) with an execution against me for the 30 _l._ 10 _s._, given the last verdict to [Field](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3815/). The man’s name is [Thomas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13726/), of [the Poultry Counter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14098/). I sent [Griffin](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1529/) with him to [the Dolphin](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/922/), where Sir W. Batten was at dinner, and he being satisfied that I should pay the money, I did cause the money to be paid him, and Griffin to tell it out to him in the office. He offered to go along with me to [Sir R. Ford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1347/), but I thought it not necessary, but let him go with it, he also telling me that there is never any receipt for it given, but I have good witness of the payment of it.

They being gone, Luellin having again told me by myself that [Deering](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7073/) is content to give me 50 _l._ if I can sell his [deals](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4992/) for him to [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/), not that I did ever offer to take it, or bid Luellin bargain for me with him, but did tacitly seem to be willing to do him what service I could in it, and expect his thanks, what he thought good.

Thence to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) by coach, by the way overtaking [Mr. Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/340/), and took him into the coach to me, and there he could tell me nothing of [my Lord](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), how he stands as to his thoughts or respect to me, but concludes that though at present he may be angry yet he will come to be pleased again with me no doubt, and says that he do mind his business well, and keeps at Court.

So to White Hall, and there by order found some of the [Commissioners of Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5243/) met, and my Lord Sandwich among the rest, to whom I bowed, but he shewed me very little if any countenance at all, which troubles me mightily.

Having soon done there, I took up Mr. Moore again and set him down at [Pauls](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/280/), by the way he proposed to me of a way of profit which perhaps may shortly be made by money by fines upon houses at [the Wardrobe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/946/), but how I did not understand but left it to another discourse.

So homeward, calling upon [Mr. Fen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1637/), by [Sir G. Carteret’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) desire, and did there shew him the bill of [Captain Taylor’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2214/) whereby I hope to get something justly.

Home and to my office, and there very late with Sir W. Warren upon very serious discourse, telling him how matters passed to-day, and in the close he and I did fall to talk very openly of the business of this office, and (if I was not a little too open to tell him my interest, which is my fault) he did give me most admirable advice, and such as do speak him a most able and worthy man, and understanding seven times more than ever I thought to be in him. He did particularly run over every one of the officers and commanders, and shewed me how I had reason to mistrust every one of them, either for their falsenesse or their over-great power, being too high to fasten a real friendship in, and did give me a common but a most excellent saying to observe in all my life. He did give it in rhyme, but the sense was this, that a man should treat every friend in his discourse and opening his mind to him as of one that may hereafter be his foe. He did also advise me how I should take occasion to make known to the world my case, and the pains that I take in my business, and above all to be sure to get a thorough knowledge in my employment, and to that add all the interest at Court that I can, which I hope I shall do.

He staid talking with me till almost 12 at night, and so good night, being sorry to part with him, and more sorry that he should have as far as [Wapping](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2469/) to walk to-night. So I to my Journall and so home, to supper and to bed.

# [Wednesday 16 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/16/)

Up, and with my head and heart full of my business, I to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and there all the morning, where among other things to my great content [Captain Taylor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2214/) brought me 40 _l._, the greater part of which I shall gain to myself after much care and pains out of his bill of freight, as I have at large set down in my book of Memorandums.

At noon to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/) and there met with [Mr. Wood](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/615/) by design, and got out of him to my advantage a condition which I shall make good use of against [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) (vide my book of Memorandums touching the contract of [masts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5619/) of [Sir W. Warren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/) about which I have had so much trouble).

So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner and then to the [Star Tavern](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1643/) hard by to our arbitration of [Mr. Bland’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5181/) business, and at it a great while, but I found no order like to be kept in our inquiry, and [Mr. Clerke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6856/), the other arbitrator, one so far from being fit (though able as to his trade of a merchant) to inquire and to take pains in searching out the truth on both sides, that we parted without doing anything, nor do I believe we shall at all ever attain to anything in it.

Then home and till 12 at night making up my accounts with great account of this day’s receipt of Captain Taylor’s money and some money reimbursed me which I have laid out on [Field’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3815/) business. So home with my mind in pretty good quiet, and to Supper and to bed.

# [Thursday 17 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/17/)

Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning. At noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to my poor [wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and dined, and then by coach abroad to [Mrs. Turner’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/121/) where I have not been for many a day, and there I found her and her sister [Dike](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7192/) very sad for the death of [their brother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/342/). After a little common expression of sorrow, Mrs. Turner told me that the trouble she would put me to was, to consult about getting an achievement prepared, [scutcheons](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7076/) were done already, to set over the door. So I did go out to [Mr. Smith’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7077/), where [my brother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/236/) tells me the scutcheons are made, but he not being within, I went to [the Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/131/), and there spent my time in a Bookseller’s shop, reading in a book of some [Embassages into Moscovia, &c.](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7078/), where was very good reading, and then to Mrs. Turner’s, and thither came Smith to me, with whom I did agree for 4 _l._ to make a handsome one, ell square within the frame. After he was gone I sat an houre talking of the suddennesse of his death within 7 days, and how by little and little death came upon him, neither he nor they thinking it would come to that. He died after a day’s raveing, through lightness in his head for want of sleep. [His lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2531/) did not know of his sickness, nor do they hear yet how she takes it.

Hence home, taking some books by the way in [Paul’s Churchyard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/821/) by coach to my office, where late doing business, and so home to supper and to bed.

# [Friday 18 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/18/)

Up, and after being ready and done several businesses with people, I took water (taking a dram of the bottle at the waterside) with a [gally](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7865/), the first that ever I had yet, and down to [Woolwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1675/), calling at [Ham Creeke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5267/), where I met [Mr. Deane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5132/), and had a great deal of talke with him about business, and so to the [Ropeyarde](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5129/) and Docke, discoursing several things, and so back again and did the like at [Deptford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1350/), and I find that it is absolutely necessary for me to do thus once a weeke at least all the yeare round, which will do me great good, and so home with great ease and content, especially out of the content which I met with in a book I bought yesterday, being a discourse of the state of Rome under the present Pope, [Alexander the 7th](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4893/), it being a very excellent piece. After eating something at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), then to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where till night about business to dispatch. Among other people came [Mr. Primate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7080/), the leather seller, in [Fleete Streete](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/127/), to see me, he says, coming this way; and he tells me that he is upon a proposal to [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/), whereby, by a law already in being, he will supply the King, without wrong to any man, or charge to the people in general, so much as it is now, above 200,000 _l._ per annum, and God knows what, and that the King do like the proposal, and hath directed that the [Duke of Monmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5315/), with their consent, be made privy, and go along with him and his fellow proposer in the business, God knows what it is; for I neither can guess nor believe there is any such thing in his head. At night made an end of the discourse I read this morning, and so home to supper and to bed.

# [Saturday 19 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/19/)

Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning, and I laboured hard at [Deering’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7073/) business of his [deals](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4992/) more than I would if I did not think to get something, though I do really believe that I did what is to [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) advantage in it, and yet, God knows, the expectation of profit will have its force and make a man the more earnest. Dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and then with [Mr. Bland](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5181/) to another meeting upon his arbitration, and seeing we were likely to do no good I even put them upon it, and they chose [Sir W. Rider](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1766/) alone to end the matter, and so I am rid of it. Thence by coach to my shoemaker’s and paid all there, and gave something to the boys’ box against [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/). To [Mrs. Turner’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/121/), whom I find busy with [Sir W. Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3725/), about advising upon going down to Norfolke with the corps, and I find him in talke a sober, considering man. So home to my office late, and then home to supper and to bed. My head full of business, but pretty good content.

# [Sunday 20 December 1663](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/12/20/)

(Lord’s day). Up and alone to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), where a common sermon of [Mr. Mills](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1215/), and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner in our parler, [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) being clean, and the first time we have dined here a great while together, and in the afternoon went to church with me also, and there begun to take her place above [Mrs. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2849/), which heretofore out of a humour she was wont to give her as an affront to my [Lady Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1572/). After a dull sermon of [the Scotchman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5805/), home, and there I found my brother [Tom](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/236/) and my two cozens Scotts, [he](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/951/) and [she](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1761/), the first time they were ever here. And by and by in comes my uncle [Wight](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/911/) and [Mr. Norbury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2724/), and they sat with us a while drinking, of [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/), of which I did give them plenty. But the two would not stay supper, but the other two did. And we were as merry as I could be with people that I do wish well to, but know not what discourse either to give them or find from them. We showed them our house from top to bottom, and had a good [Turkey](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/378/) roasted for our supper, and store of wine, and after supper sent them home on foot, and so we to prayers and to bed.
