# [Wednesday 20 December 1665](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1665/12/20/)

Up, and was trimmed, but not time enough to save my [Lord Bruncker’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) coach or [Sir J. Minnes’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/), and so was fain to walk to [Lambeth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1265/) on foot, but it was a very fine frosty walke, and great pleasure in it, but troublesome getting over [the River](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1832/) for ice. I to the [Duke of Albemarle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/), whither my brethren were all come, but I was not too late. There we sat in discourse upon our Navy business an houre, and thence in my Lord Bruncker’s coach alone, he walking before (while I staid awhile talking with [Sir G. Downing](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/106/) about the Act, in which he is horrid troublesome) to the [Old Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/). Thence I took [Sir Ellis Layton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7163/) to [Captain Cocke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), where my Lord Bruncker and [Lady Williams](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8925/) dine, and we all mighty merry; but Sir Ellis Layton one of the best companions at a meale in the world. After dinner I to [the Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/) to see whether [my pretty seamstress](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8438/) be come again or no, and I find she is, so I to her, saluted her over her counter in the open Exchange above, and mightily joyed to see her, poor pretty woman! I must confess I think her a great beauty. After laying out a little money there for two pair of thread stockings, cost 8 _s._, I to [Lumbard Streete](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/966/) to see some business to-night there at the goldsmith’s, among others paying in 1258 _l._ to [Viner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8584/) for my [Lord Sandwich’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) use upon Cocke’s account. I was called by my Lord Bruncker in his coach with his mistresse, and [Mr. Cottle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9529/) the lawyer, our acquaintance at [Greenwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2673/), and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) to Greenwich, and thence I to [Mrs. Penington](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9050/), and had a supper from the [King’s Head](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9015/) for her, and there mighty merry and free as I used to be with her, and at last, late, I did pray her to undress herself into her nightgowne, that I might see how to have her picture drawne carelessly (for she is mighty proud of that conceit), and I would walk without in the streete till she had done. So I did walk forth, and whether I made too many turns or no in the darke cold frosty night between the two walls up to the Parke gate I know not, but she was gone to bed when I come again to the house, upon pretence of leaving some papers there, which I did on purpose by her consent. So I away home, and was there sat up for to be spoken with my young [Mrs. Daniel](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9099/), to pray me to speake for [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9530/) to be a Lieutenant. I had the opportunity here of kissing her again and again, and did answer that I would be very willing to do him any kindnesse, and so parted, and I to bed, exceedingly pleased in all my matters of money this month or two, it having pleased God to bless me with several opportunities of good sums, and that I have them in effect all very well paid, or in my power to have. But two things trouble me; one, [the sicknesse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/301/) is increased above 80 this weeke (though in my owne parish not one has died, though six the last weeke); the other, most of all, which is, that I have so complexed an account for these last two months for variety of layings out upon [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/), occasions and variety of gettings that I have not made even with myself now these 3 or 4 months, which do trouble me mightily, finding that I shall hardly ever come to understand them thoroughly again, as I used to do my accounts when I was at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/).

# [Thursday 21 December 1665](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1665/12/21/)

At [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8991/) all the morning. At noon all of us dined at [Captain Cocke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/) at a good [chine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1705/) of [beef](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/381/), and other good meat; but, being all frost-bitten, was most of it unroast; but very merry, and a good dish of fowle we dressed ourselves. [Mr. Evelyn](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1033/) there, in very good humour. All the afternoon till night pleasant, and then I took my leave of them and to the office, where I wrote my letters, and away [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/), my head full of business and some trouble for my letting my accounts go so far that I have made an oathe this night for the drinking no [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/), &c., on such penalties till I have passed my accounts and cleared all. Coming home and going to bed, the boy tells me his sister [Daniel](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9099/) has provided me a supper of little birds killed by [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9530/), and I made her sup with me, and after supper were alone a great while, and I had the pleasure of her lips, she being a pretty woman, and one whom a great belly becomes as well as ever I saw any. She gone, I to bed. This day I was come to by [Mrs. Burrows](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8607/), of Westminster, [Lieutenant Burrows](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9531/) (lately dead) [his wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8607/), a most pretty woman and my old acquaintance; I had a kiss or two of her, and a most modest woman she is.

# [Friday 22 December 1665](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1665/12/22/)

Up betimes and to my [Lord Bruncker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) to consider the late instructions sent us for the method of our signing bills hereafter and paying them. By and by, by agreement, comes [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) and [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/), and then to read them publicly and consider of putting them in execution. About this all the morning, and, it appearing necessary for the Controller to have another Clerke, I recommended [Poynter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9464/) to him, which he accepts, and I by that means rid of one that I fear would not have been fit for my turne, though he writes very well. At noon comes [Mr. Hill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7165/) to towne, and finds me out here, and brings [Mr. Houbland](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8247/), who met him here. So I was compelled to leave my Lord and his dinner and company, and with them to [the Beare](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9533/), and dined with them and their brothers, of which Hill had his and the other two [of](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9534/)[his](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9535/), and mighty merry and very fine company they are, and I glad to see them. After dinner I forced to take leave of them by being called upon by [Mr. Andrews](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7673/), I having sent for him, and by a fine glosse did bring him to desire [tallys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8499/) for what orders I have to pay him and his company for [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) victualls, and I by that means cleared to myself 210 _l._ coming to me upon their two orders, which is also a noble addition to my late profits, which have been very considerable of late, but how great I know not till I come to cast up my accounts, which burdens my mind that it should be so backward, but I am resolved to settle to nothing till I have done it.

He gone, I to my Lord Bruncker’s, and there spent the evening by my desire in seeing his Lordship open to pieces and make up again his [watch](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/715/), thereby being taught what I never knew before; and it is a thing very well worth my having seen, and am mightily pleased and satisfied with it. So I sat talking with him till late at night, somewhat vexed at a snappish answer [Madam Williams](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8925/) did give me to herself, upon my speaking a free word to her in mirthe, calling her a mad jade. She answered, we were not so well acquainted yet. But I was more at a letter from my [Lord Duke of Albemarle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/) to-day, pressing us to continue our meetings for all [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/), which, though every body intended not to have done, yet I am concluded in it, who intended nothing else. But I see it is necessary that I do make often visits to my Lord Duke, which nothing shall hinder after I have evened my accounts, and now [the river](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1832/) is frozen I know not how to get to him.

Thence to my lodging, making up my Journall for 8 or 9 days, and so my mind being eased of it, I to supper and to bed.

The weather hath been frosty these eight or nine days, and so we hope for an abatement of [the plague](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/301/) the next weeke, or else God have mercy upon us! for the plague will certainly continue the next year if it do not.

# [Saturday 23 December 1665](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1665/12/23/)

At [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8991/) all the morning and [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) to dinner, my head full of business, and there [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) finds me unexpectedly. But I not being at leisure to stay or talk with her, she went down by coach to [Woolwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1675/), thinking to fetch [Mrs. Barbary](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8955/) to carry her to London to keep her [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/) with her, and I to the office. This day one come to me with four great [turkies](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/378/), as a present from [Mr. Deane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5132/), at [Harwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7985/), three of which my wife carried in the evening [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) with her to London in her coach (Mrs. Barbary not being to be got so suddenly, but will come to her the next week), and I at my office late, and then to my lodgings to bed.

# [Sunday 24 December 1665](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1665/12/24/)

(Sunday). Up betimes, to my [Lord Duke of Albemarle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/) by water, and after some talke with him about business of the office with great content, and so back again and to dinner, [my landlady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9069/) and [her](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9099/)[daughters](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9102/) with me, and had [mince-pies](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3371/), and very merry at a mischance her [young son](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9402/) had in tearing of his new coate quite down the outside of his sleeve in the whole cloth, one of the strangest mishaps that ever I saw in my life. Then to church, and placed myself in the Parson’s pew under the pulpit, to hear [Mrs. Chamberlain](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9469/) in the next pew sing, who is daughter to [Sir James Bunch](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9466/), of whom I have heard much, and indeed she sings very finely, and from church met with [Sir W. Warren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/) and he and I walked together talking about his and my businesses, getting of money as fairly as we can, and, having set him part of his way home, I walked to my [Lord Bruncker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/), whom I heard was at [Alderman Hooker’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8904/), hoping to see and salute [Mrs. Lethulier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9470/), whom I did see in passing, but no opportunity of beginning acquaintance, but a very noble lady she is, however the silly alderman got her. Here we sat talking a great while, [Sir The. Biddulph](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8122/) and [Mr. Vaughan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9536/), a son-in-law of [Alderman Hooker’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8904/). Hence with my Lord Bruncker home and sat a little with him and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) to bed.

# [Monday 25 December 1665](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1665/12/25/)

([Christmas-day](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/)). To church in the morning, and there saw a wedding in the church, which I have not seen many a day; and the young people so merry one with another, and strange to see what delight we married people have to see these poor fools decoyed into our condition, every man and woman gazing and smiling at them. Here I saw again my beauty [Lethulier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9470/). Thence to my [Lord Bruncker’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) by invitation and dined there, and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) to look over and settle my papers, both of my accounts private, and those of [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/), which I have let go so long that it were impossible for any soul, had I died, to understand them, or ever come to any good end in them. I hope God will never suffer me to come to that disorder again.

# [Tuesday 26 December 1665](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1665/12/26/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8991/), where [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) and my [Lord Bruncker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) and I met, to give our directions to the Commanders of all the ships in [the river](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1832/) to bring in lists of their ships’ companies, with entries, discharges, &c., all the last voyage, where young [Seymour](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9550/), among 20 that stood bare, stood with his hat on, a proud, saucy young man. Thence with them to [Mr. Cuttle’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9529/), being invited, and dined nobly and neatly; with a very pretty house and a fine turret at top, with winding stairs and the finest prospect I know about all [Greenwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2673/), save the top of the hill, and yet in some respects better than that. Here I also saw some fine writing worke and flourishing of [Mr. Hore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/765/), he one that I knew long ago, an acquaintance of [Mr. Tomson’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9551/) at Westminster, that is this man’s clerk. It is the story of the several Archbishops of Canterbury, engrossed in vellum, to hang up in [Canterbury Cathedrall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9552/) in tables, in lieu of the old ones, which are almost worn out. Thence to the office a while, and so to [Captain Cocke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/) and there talked, and [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) to look over my papers, and so to bed.

# [Wednesday 27 December 1665](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1665/12/27/)

Up, and with [Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), by coach to London, there [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), and angry about her desiring a mayde yet, before [the plague](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/301/) is quite over. It seems [Mercer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7761/) is troubled that she hath not one under her, but I will not venture my family by increasing it before it be safe. Thence about many businesses, particularly with [Sir W. Warren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/) on the [’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and he and I dined together and settled our [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) matters, wherein I get above 200 _l._ presently. We dined together at the [Pope’s Head](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9544/) to do this, and thence to the goldsmiths, I to examine the state of my matters there too, and so with him to my house, but my wife was gone abroad to [Mrs. Mercer’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7967/), so we took boat, and it being darke and the thaw having broke the ice, but not carried it quite away, the boat did pass through so much of it all along, and that with the crackling and noise that it made me fearfull indeed. So I forced the watermen to land us on [Redriffe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2301/) side, and so walked together till Sir W. Warren and I parted near his house and thence I walked quite over the fields home by light of [linke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1167/), one of my watermen carrying it, and I reading by the light of it, it being a very fine, clear, dry night. So to Captain Cocke’s, and there sat and talked, especially with his Counsellor, about his [prize goods](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9633/), that hath done him good turne, being of the company with [Captain Fisher](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9067/), his name [Godderson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9553/); here I supped and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) to bed, with great content that the plague is decreased to 152, the whole being but 330.

# [Thursday 28 December 1665](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1665/12/28/)

Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8991/), and thence with a great deal of business in my head, dined alone with [Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/). So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) alone strictly about my accounts, wherein I made a good beginning, and so, after letters wrote by the post, to bed.

# [Friday 29 December 1665](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1665/12/29/)

Up betimes, and all day long within doors upon my accounts, publique and private, and find the ill effect of letting them go so long without evening, that no soul could have ever understood them but myself, and I with much ado. But, however, my regularity in all I did and spent do helpe me, and I hope to find them well. Late at them and to bed.

# [Saturday 30 December 1665](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1665/12/30/)

Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8991/), at noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) to dinner, and all the afternoon to my accounts again, and there find myself, to my great joy, a great deal [worth above 4000 _l._](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9548/), for which the Lord be praised! and is principally occasioned by my getting 500 _l._ of [Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), for my profit in his bargains of [prize goods](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9633/), and from [Mr. Gawden’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/994/) making me a present of 500 _l._ more, when I paid him 8000 for [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/). So to my office to write letters, then to my accounts again, and so to bed, being in great ease of mind.

# [Sunday 31 December 1665](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1665/12/31/)

(Lord’s day). All the morning in my chamber, writing fair the state of my [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) accounts, and so dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/). In the afternoon to the [Duke of Albemarle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/) and thence back again by water, and so to my chamber to finish the entry of my accounts and to think of the business I am next to do, which is the stating my thoughts and putting in order my collections about the business of pursers, to see where the fault of our present constitution relating to them lies and what to propose to mend it, and upon this late and with my head full of this business to bed. Thus ends this year, to my great joy, in this manner.

I have raised my estate from 1300 _l._ in this year [to 4400 _l._](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9548/). I have got myself greater interest, I think, by my diligence, and my employments encreased by that of [Treasurer for Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8408/), and [Surveyour of the Victualls](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9082/).

It is true we have gone through great melancholy because of the great [plague](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/301/), and I put to great charges by it, by keeping my family long at [Woolwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1675/), and myself and another part of my family, my clerks, at my charge at [Greenwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2673/), and a mayde at London; but I hope [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) will give us some satisfaction for that. But now the plague is abated almost to nothing, and I intending to get to London as fast as I can. My family, that is [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and maids, having been there these two or three weeks. The Dutch war goes on very ill, by reason of lack of money; having none to hope for, all being put into disorder by [a new Act](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14126/) that is made as an experiment to bring credit to the [Exchequer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/290/), for goods and money to be advanced upon the credit of that Act. I have never lived so merrily (besides that I never got so much) as I have done this plague time, by my [Lord Bruncker’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) and [Captain Cocke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/) good company, and the acquaintance of [Mrs. Knipp](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9483/), [Coleman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9387/) and [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9386/), and [Mr. Laneare](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9388/), and great store of dancings we have had at my cost (which I was willing to indulge myself and wife) at [my lodgings](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/). The great evil of this year, and the only one indeed, is the fall of my [Lord of Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), whose mistake about the [prizes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9633/) hath undone him, I believe, as to interest at Court; though sent (for a little palliating it) Embassador into Spayne, which he is now fitting himself for. But the Duke of Albemarle goes with [the Prince](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1357/) to sea this next year, and my Lord very meanly spoken of; and, indeed, his miscarriage about the prize goods is not to be excused, to suffer a company of rogues to go away with ten times as much as himself, and the blame of all to be deservedly laid upon him.1

My whole family hath been well all this while, and all my friends I know of, saving my [aunt Bell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1104/), who is dead, and some children of my [cozen Sarah’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3004/), of the plague. But many of such as I know very well, dead; yet, to our great joy, the town fills apace, and shops begin to be open again. Pray God continue the plague’s decrease! for that keeps the Court away from the place of business, and so all goes to rack as to publick matters, they at this distance not thinking of it.

1.   According to Granville Penn (“Memorials of Sir W. Penn,” ii. 488 n.) 2000 _l._ went to Lord Sandwich and 8000 _l._ among eight others. ↩

# Sunday 2 December 1660

(Lord’s day). My head not very well, and my body out of order by last night’s drinking, which is my great folly. To [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), and [Mr. Mills](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1215/) made a good sermon; so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner. [My wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I all alone to a leg of [mutton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1740/), the sawce of which being made sweet, I was angry at it, and eat none, but only dined upon the marrow bone that we had beside.

To church in the afternoon, and after sermon took [Tom Fuller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/806/)[Church History](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1752/) and read over [Henry the 8th’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5978/) life in it, and so to supper and to bed.

# Sunday 2 December 1660

(Lord’s day). My head not very well, and my body out of order by last night’s drinking, which is my great folly. To [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), and [Mr. Mills](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1215/) made a good sermon; so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner. [My wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I all alone to a leg of [mutton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1740/), the sawce of which being made sweet, I was angry at it, and eat none, but only dined upon the marrow bone that we had beside.

To church in the afternoon, and after sermon took [Tom Fuller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/806/)[Church History](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1752/) and read over [Henry the 8th’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5978/) life in it, and so to supper and to bed.

# Tuesday 10 December 1661

To [Whitehall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there finding [Mons. Eschar](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/831/) to be gone, I sent my letters by a porter to the posthouse in [Southwark](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1284/) to be sent by despatch to [the Downs](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1257/). So to dinner to my [Lord Crew’s](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/105/) by coach, and in my way had a [stop](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10533/) of above an hour and a half, which is a great trouble this [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) time, but it cannot be helped. However I got thither before my Lord come from [the House](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/293/), and so dined with him, and dinner done, home to the [office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and there sat late and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/).

### [emvee107](https://www.pepysdiary.com/account/profile/3584/ "See more about this person")on 2 Jan 2025•Link

For San Diego Sarah. Re 'Plying in the mouth of the Gut -- The Assistance'.   
In Malta, the entrance to Marsamxett Harbour is between the headlands on which the towns of Sliema and Valetta are situated. Protecting the entrance are Fort Tigne and Fort St. Elmo. By Fort Tigne is a viewpoint called 'Il-Ponta ta' Dragut', and a few hundred yards offshore is the Dragutt Shoal. I spent a few months in Malta nearly 50 years ago, courtesy of the Queen In Valetta there is Strait Street, affectionately known as 'The Gut' to sailors and other travellers, which provided, (probably still does), refreshment and entertainment appreciated by the above mentioned.   
Not conclusive I agree,but I am not aware of any other places referred to as 'the Gut' in the Med. I remain open-minded. Hope this helps.

# Tuesday 10 December 1661

To [Whitehall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there finding [Mons. Eschar](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/831/) to be gone, I sent my letters by a porter to the posthouse in [Southwark](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1284/) to be sent by despatch to [the Downs](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1257/). So to dinner to my [Lord Crew’s](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/105/) by coach, and in my way had a [stop](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10533/) of above an hour and a half, which is a great trouble this [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) time, but it cannot be helped. However I got thither before my Lord come from [the House](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/293/), and so dined with him, and dinner done, home to the [office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and there sat late and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/).

Ds. is not a title, but a Latin abbreviation.  
In the dictionary of Latin common abbreviations (see: [asgle.classics.unc.edu/abbrev/lat…](http://asgle.classics.unc.edu/abbrev/latin/Popd.htm))  
we see that Ds stands for one of the following:  
d(e) s, d(e) s(ua), d(e) s(uis), d(e) s(uo), d(e)s(ignatum), d(ecreto) s(enatus), d(ecurionum) s(ententia), D(eo) S(aturno), D(eo) S(oli), D(eu)s, D(i)s, d(ie) s(exto), d(ie)s, d(iebu)s, d(iscens) s(ignifer), d(iscens) s(igniferorum), d(omini)s, D(omino) s(ancto) . It is for us now to find out which of this abbreviations is the right one.  
I think it may be "De Signatum", meaning that Lord Crewe (and others) sent a signed note excusing themself for some reason (illness, etc.).

"Epus." is another Latin abbreviation that I do not know how to interpret, but must be similar in some way.

I hope some of our readers knows better and shares is knowledge with us.

For San Diego Sarah. Re 'Plying in the mouth of the Gut -- The Assistance'.   
In Malta, the entrance to Marsamxett Harbour is between the headlands on which the towns of Sliema and Valetta are situated. Protecting the entrance are Fort Tigne and Fort St. Elmo. I spent a few months in Malta nearly 50 years ago, courtesy of the Queen In Valetta there is Strait Street, affectionately known as 'The Gut' to sailors and other travellers, which provided, (probably still does), refreshment and entertainment appreciated by the above mentioned.   
Not conclusive I agree,but I am not aware of any other places referred to as 'the Gut' in the Med. I remain open-minded. Hope this helps.

# Saturday 1 December 1660

This morning, observing some things to be laid up not as they should be by [the girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/149/), I took a broom and basted her till she cried extremely, which made me vexed, but before I went out I left her appeased. So to [Whitehall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), where I found [Mr. Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/340/) attending for me at [the Privy Seal](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/900/), but nothing to do to-day.

I went to my [Lord St. Albans](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1618/) lodgings, and found him in bed, talking to a priest (he looked like one) that leaned along over the side of the bed, and there I desired to know his mind about making the [catch](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9392/) stay longer, which I got ready for him the other day. He seems to be a fine civil gentleman.

To [my Lord’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), and did give up my audit of his accounts, which I had been then two days about, and was well received by my Lord. I dined with my Lord and [Lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/), and we had a [venison pasty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/384/). [Mr. Shepley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/118/) and I went into London, and calling upon [Mr. Pinkney](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1641/), the goldsmith, he took us to the tavern, and gave us a pint of [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/), and there fell into our company old [Mr. Flower](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13978/) and another gentleman; who tell us how a Scotch knight was killed basely the other day at [the Fleece](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1642/) in [Covent Garden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/126/), where there had been a great many formerly killed. So to [Paul’s Churchyard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/182/), and there I took the little man at [Mr. Kirton’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1539/) and [Mr. Shepley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/118/) to Ringstead’s at [the Star](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1643/), and after a pint of wine I went [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), my brains somewhat troubled with so much wine, and after a letter or two by the post I went to bed.

Pepys and Papists

St. Albans (according to a note for this date in the L&M version), was "one of the leading Catholics at Court." At the beginning of 1660, wouldn't it have been close to unthinkable that a Catholic would be an influential member of the governing circles, even favored by the head of state?

It's easy to imagine a modern equivalent of Pepys's reaction: A member of a frequently despised minority group moves next door and you're soon in a conversation with someone who reports a little breathlessly that the new neighbor is "really very nice." But alert eyes have spotted something that just might be one of those things that would send the bigots up the wall (in Pepys's case a possible priest sighting -- right in the home of an influential Londoner! Wouldn't Pepys's mother be scandalized!).

Wouldn't some (a few of Pepys's old drinking buddies, for instance) be suspicious of Catholics in high office, and wonder if they might be agents of the Pope? And here's the ambassador to Catholic France, no less! But this is after the revolution, and none dare call it treason -- it's the Puritans who have to watch themselves.

# Saturday 1 December 1660

This morning, observing some things to be laid up not as they should be by [the girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/149/), I took a broom and basted her till she cried extremely, which made me vexed, but before I went out I left her appeased. So to [Whitehall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), where I found [Mr. Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/340/) attending for me at [the Privy Seal](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/900/), but nothing to do to-day.

I went to my [Lord St. Albans](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1618/) lodgings, and found him in bed, talking to a priest (he looked like one) that leaned along over the side of the bed, and there I desired to know his mind about making the [catch](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9392/) stay longer, which I got ready for him the other day. He seems to be a fine civil gentleman.

To [my Lord’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), and did give up my audit of his accounts, which I had been then two days about, and was well received by my Lord. I dined with my Lord and [Lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/), and we had a [venison pasty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/384/). [Mr. Shepley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/118/) and I went into London, and calling upon [Mr. Pinkney](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1641/), the goldsmith, he took us to the tavern, and gave us a pint of [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/), and there fell into our company old [Mr. Flower](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13978/) and another gentleman; who tell us how a Scotch knight was killed basely the other day at [the Fleece](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1642/) in [Covent Garden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/126/), where there had been a great many formerly killed. So to [Paul’s Churchyard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/182/), and there I took the little man at [Mr. Kirton’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1539/) and [Mr. Shepley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/118/) to Ringstead’s at [the Star](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1643/), and after a pint of wine I went [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), my brains somewhat troubled with so much wine, and after a letter or two by the post I went to bed.

Wouldn't some (a few of Pepys's old drinking buddies, for instance) be suspicious of Catholics in high office, and wonder if they might be agents of the Pope? Puritans and Christmas  
The Puritans wanted to strip away all the "superstitious" parts of Christian observance that had grown up over the years and get back to a pure religion based solely on the Bible and what they imagined the early Church to be like. They were particularly hostile towards icons, statues, and the veneration of the saints (along with their holy days), which they saw as akin to idolatry. They thought that all the holy day traditions, including Christmas festivities, as excuses for revelry, when people should be praying and studying the word of God.

### [Sasha Clarkson](https://www.pepysdiary.com/account/profile/23/ "See more about this person")on 1 Dec 2013•Link

The traditional country celebrations of Christmas did indeed have pagan roots, which were merely rebranded by the early and mediaeval church. For example, carols like 'The Holly And The Ivy', and 'The Boar's Head', refer to pagan customs.

The boar was sacred to the Norse/Germanic fertility god Freyr/Frey, and also to his sister Freyja. At Yule, the Norse winter solstice festival, it was traditional to sacrifice a boar to Freyr. I would imagine, the pagans being practical people, that the head would have been the god's portion, whilst the village folk ate the rest!

"I went to my Lord St. Albans lodgings, and found him in bed, talking to a priest (he looked like one) that leaned along over the side of the bed, and there I desired to know his mind about making the catch stay longer, which I got ready for him the other day. He seems to be a fine civil gentleman."

Pepys may have been aware of the gossip about Henry Jermyn, Earl of St. Albans:  
'Gossip which the historian Henry Hallam accepted as authentic, but which is supported by no real evidence, asserted that Jermyn was secretly married to Queen Henrietta Maria during their exile in France. It was further rumoured during Jermyn's lifetime that he may have been the true father of at least one of her children, even perhaps of Charles II.   
"The Domestic State Papers for 13 August, 1660, contain a report by Capt. Francis Robinson of Nathaniel Angelo, a Windsor clergyman, asserting that "all the royal children were Jermyn's bastards."'  
[www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/08/…](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/08/13/#c558093)

Most Englishmen were very wary of anything and everything French (almost a code word for Roman Catholic), and St. Albans was the leading advocate of all things French.

Pepys assuming that the man was a priest is not surprising.

Sandwich had asked Pepys to order the ketch when the Queen Mother, Minette and St. Albans were imminently supposed to return to France. This sounds as if Sandwich was not authorized to release the ketch, although everyone knew their return was rescheduled until next year.  
[www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/11/…](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/11/22/)

Evidently, St. Albans was grateful for Sandwich and Pepys' care, and was respectful of Pepys' time.

# Friday 1 December 1665

This morning to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8991/), full of resolution to spend the whole day at business, and there, among other things, I did agree with [Poynter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9464/) to be my clerke for my [Victualling](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9960/) business, and so all alone all the day long shut up in my little closett at my office, drawing up instructions, which I should long since have done for my Surveyours of the Ports, [Sir W. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) desiring much to have them, and he might well have expected them long since. After dinner to it again, and at night had long discourse with [Gibson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9465/), who is for [Yarmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/578/), who makes me understand so much of the victualling business and the pursers’ trade, that I am ashamed I should go about the concerning myself in a business which I understand so very very little of, and made me distrust all I had been doing to-day. So I did lay it by till to-morrow morning to think of it afresh, and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8994/) by promise to [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), to have mirth there. So we had our neighbours, little [Miss Tooker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9070/) and [Mrs. Daniels](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9099/), to dance, and after supper I to bed, and left them merry below, which they did not part from till two or three in the morning.

# Saturday 2 December 1665

Up, and discoursing with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), who is resolved to go to London for good and all this day, we did agree upon giving [Mr. Sheldon](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5055/) 10 _l._, and [Mrs. Barbary](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8955/) two pieces, and so I left her to go down thither to fetch away the rest of the things and pay him the money, and so I to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8991/), where very busy setting [Mr. Poynter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9464/) to write out my last night’s worke, which pleases me this day, but yet it is pretty to reflect how much I am out of confidence with what I had done upon [Gibson’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9465/) discourse with me, for fear I should have done it sillily, but Poynter likes them, and [Mr. Hater](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1026/) also, but yet I am afeard lest they should do it out of flattery, so conscious I am of my ignorance.

Dined with my wife at noon and took leave of her, she being to go to London, as I said, for altogether, and I to the office, busy till past one in the morning.

# Saturday 2 December 1665

Up, and discoursing with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), who is resolved to go to London for good and all this day, we did agree upon giving [Mr. Sheldon](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5055/) 10 _l._, and [Mrs. Barbary](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8955/) two pieces, and so I left her to go down thither to fetch away the rest of the things and pay him the money, and so I to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8991/), where very busy setting [Mr. Poynter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9464/) to write out my last night’s worke, which pleases me this day, but yet it is pretty to reflect how much I am out of confidence with what I had done upon [Gibson’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9465/) discourse with me, for fear I should have done it sillily, but Poynter likes them, and [Mr. Hater](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1026/) also, but yet I am afeard lest they should do it out of flattery, so conscious I am of my ignorance.

Dined with my wife at noon and took leave of her, she being to go to London, as I said, for altogether, and I to the office, busy till past one in the morning.

# Saturday 13 December 1662

Slept long to-day till [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) and [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) were set out towards [Portsmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1764/) before I rose, and [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) came to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) to speak with me before I was up. So I started up and down to him. By and by we sat, [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) and I (Sir G. Carteret being gone), and among other things, [Field](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3815/) and [Stint](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5701/) did come, and received the 41 _l._ given him by the judgement against me and [Harry Kem](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5702/);1 and we did also sign bonds in 500 _l._ to stand to the award of [Mr. Porter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5703/) and [Smith](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1345/) for the rest: which, however, I did not sign to till I got Mr. Coventry to go up with me to [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/); and he did promise me before him to bear his share in what should be awarded, and both concluded that Sir W. Batten would do no less. At noon broke up and dined with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), and then to the office again, and there made an end of last night’s examination, and got my study there made very clean and put in order, and then to write by the post, among other letters one to Sir W. Batten about this day’s work with Field, desiring his promise also. The letter I have caused to be entered in our public book of letters. So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to supper and to bed.

1.   Fine for the imprisonment of Field (see [February 4th, 1661-62](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1662/02/04/), and [October 21st, 1662](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1662/10/21/)). ↩

Peruque - Sam is still wearing his own hair at this time!

# January 1664

Sam’s New Year begins with the “bill of exchange” from Deering via Luellin which finds an ebullient Sam 50 _l._ richer, yet still rationalizing the ethics of this and potential future ‘payments’ ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/01/), [5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/05/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/25/)). His New Year happily brings the end to his vow against plays. Sam’s disappointment upon seeing the much touted “Henry VIII” ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/01/)) and “The Usurper” ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/02/)) are followed by a vow to limit the number of plays he will see per month ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/02/)). Not to be at a loss for “entertainment” Sam finds himself highly interested in the case of the stolen jewels of Mr. Tyran, an “old man, a merchant” ([8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/08/)). As the case unfolds, a Colonel Turner is accused, tried and hanged with an estimate of 12-14,000 people, including Sam, attending the execution ([10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/10/), [16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/16/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/20/), [21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/21/)).

Sam’s concern about his relationship with Lord Sandwich continues. He ponders inviting “my Lord” to dinner, but as their exchanges over the month unfold Sam thinks it best to “forbear my laying out my money upon a dinner till I see him in a better posture” ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/09/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/20/)). Where his relationship with Sandwich feels unsure, his relationship with Mrs. Lane becomes more intimate ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/09/), [11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/11/), [16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/16/)). Although his visits to her bring Sam sexual fulfillment they also may be the cause of his growing but unfounded jealousy towards Elizabeth. His jealous concerns over Will and Pembleton ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/09/), [17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/17/), [18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/18/), [28](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/28/)) leave Sam to confess his irrational fears: “God knows I have no reason to do so, or to expect her being so true to me as I would have to her ([18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/18/)). By month end he does follow through on his promise to Elizabeth and finishes his will ([20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/20/), [23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/23/), [24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/24/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/25/), [28](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/28/), [30](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/30/)). While Sam’s jealousy reigns against the younger men in Elizabeth’s life Sam can only think good of Uncle Wight who seems mysteriously and overly interested to know if Elizabeth is with child. Sam hopefully believes that Uncle Wight intends to leave something to them in his will ([12](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/12/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/15/), [21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/21/)). In other family matters, brother Tom’s health seems to have taken a turn for the worse, with worries that he is in a deep consumption ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/09/), [10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/10/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/20/)).

In the Royal circles Sam watches the King’s tennis match noting his disgust at the false flattery given the monarch “but to see how the King’s play was extolled without any cause at all, was a loathsome sight, though sometimes, indeed, he did play very well and deserved to be commended; but such open flattery is beastly” ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/04/)). Sam is likewise unimpressed by the King’s lewd response to a Quaker girl who has brought forth a warrant ([11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/11/)). Mr. Pierce tells Sam the seedy gossip that Lady Castlemaine is “out” as the King now dallies openly with Frances Stuart and that the Duke of Monmouth is treated like a “Prince of the Blood”. Mr. Pierce shares the flattering opinion that the Duke of York “do give himself up to business, and is like to prove a noble Prince” to which Sam heartily agrees that “I do from my heart think he will” ([20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/20/)).

# February 1664

Talk of the growing tension between the English and the Dutch circulates ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/02/), [9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/09/)) with the Dutch proclaiming that they are the “Soveraigne of all the South Seas” ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/15/)). Business concerns include issues regarding the quality of masts ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/16/), [17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/17/), [18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/18/), [21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/21/), [22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/22/)); a letter on the behalf of Mr. Barrow ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/16/)); Mr. Maes’ customs issue ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/04/), [10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/10/)); hempe and trade ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/24/)); Creed and his pieces of eight ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/04/), [10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/10/)); a review of Lord Peterborough’s accounts ([13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/13/), [18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/18/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/25/), [26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/26/), [27](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/27/)) and a detailed report on the state of England’s Revenues by Sir Phillip Warwick, which totally captivates Sam ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/29/)). Sam benefits from his position through a gifts from Sir W. Warren ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/02/)), Mr. Falconer ([11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/11/)), and Mrs. Russell.

Elizabeth brings news that Balty and his wife will leave for his soldier duty in Holland ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/03/)). Uncle Wright’s “caresses” and private visits to Elizabeth leave Sam to believe that “it looks strange putting all together, but yet I am in hopes he means well” ([19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/19/), [22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/22/), [26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/26/)). The concerns that Sam had early in the month that he may have gotten Mrs. Lane pregnant ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/01/)) were not put at ease when the marriage that he was hoping to arrange between her and Hawley seems to fall apart ([8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/08/)). Sam vows that he is now “resolved wholly to avoid occasion of further ill with her” ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/29/)). His receives advice from Mr. Howe regarding his relationship with Lord Sandwich ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/03/), [8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/08/)). Howe “did of himself advise me to appear more free with my Lord and to come to him, for my own strangeness he tells me he thinks do make my Lord the worse.” ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/29/))

Court gossip includes the Duke’s new perriwigg ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/15/)), Lady Castlemaine’s theater antics ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/01/)), the scathing condition of foreign policy, pathetic internal court politics, and a deep concern for the overall welfare of England under King Charles II ([22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/22/)). On a more playful note, Sam enjoys seeing “The Indian Queene” with Elizabeth ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/01/)), buying two books ([22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/22/)), observing sand, louse and mites under a microscope ([13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/13/)), watching marble being cut ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/24/)) and receiving a new mastiffe named “Towser” ([17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/17/)) who he thinks he will give to his father as a present ([18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/18/)).

# March 1664

March begins on an upbeat note as Lord Sandwich praises Sam to Lord Peterborough and Povy ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/03/)). Lord Sandwich’s favour also yields Sam’s a role as an assistant under the Duke of York in the newly created Corporation of the Royal Fishery ([10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/10/)). Sam celebrates the new month by bending his vows to see two plays, “The Unfortunate Lovers” and “Heraclius” ([7](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/07/), [8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/08/)).

Happiness is short lived when Tom takes a turn for the worse. When Mrs. Turner’s son arrives with a note that Tom’s illness may be the pox ([13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/13/)), Sam is rightly upset regarding such shameful accusations. Sam visits Tom several times over the following days as his health deteriorates. Sam assists as two different doctors check Tom’s body for signs of the pox, but there are none, which offer Sam some relief ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/15/)). Meanwhile Sam starts to gather details regarding the nature of Tom’s lifestyle, including his debts, mysterious meetings with Cave and Cranburne, and his bad husbandry ([13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/13/), [14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/14/)). Tom passes away, and amidst funeral preparations, Sam discovers among Tom’s papers some back-stabbing letters written about him by his brother John ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/15/)). Sam’s father arrives a “poor man, very sad and sickly,” and has barely a moment to grieve before an angry Sam confronts him about the content of John’s letters ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/16/), [18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/18/), [19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/19/), [21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/21/)). As the days progress, Sam seeks advice from Mr. Moore regarding who should administer Tom’s estate ([27](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/27/)).

Among the despair, a hilarious lightness is found when Sam decides that Mrs. Buggin’s decidedly beautiful dog should mate with his bitch and he helps him along ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/23/), [24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/24/)). The month ends at Sam’s house with a happy dinner gathering as Sam celebrates his “solemn feast” for the cutting of his stone ([26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/26/)).

# April 1664

April brings continued efforts to settle brother Tom’s estate ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/16/)) and the shocking surprise that Tom had fathered a daughter with his maid Margaret ([6](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/06/)). Concerns over a potential Dutch war overwhelm many of Sam’s conversations ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/04/), [13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/13/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/20/), [23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/23/)). While Howe and others plot for a favored spot should war begin ([12](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/12/)), Sam’s fears for the safety of his accounts, which could be lost, should Lord Sandwich perish in battle ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/23/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/25/), [26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/26/)). The month ends with a more impending concern over loss of life when Lady Sandwich, Sam’s favourite, becomes ill with either the measles or, as Sam fears, perhaps smallpox ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/29/), [30](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/30/)).

# May 1664

Navy work includes Sam’s ongoing disgust with Sir W. Batten ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/03/), [5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/05/), [22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/22/), [26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/26/)); discussions of the possibility of a Dutch War with Coventry ([12](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/12/), [18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/18/), [21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/21/), [22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/22/), [29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/29/)); his bribe from Captain Taylor ([27](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/27/)); his interest in shipbuilding ([7](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/07/), [13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/13/), [30](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/30/)); and his unusual role as a go-between to elicit Lord Sandwich (at Coventry’s request) to see if he would go to sea under the Duke of York should war with the Dutch prevail ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/29/),31).

In personal matters Sam is relieved to find Lady Sandwich on the mend ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/09/), [12](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/12/)) and thrilled that work on his closet was done so well ([6](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/06/)). On the more worrisome side, he notes the death of Uncle Fenner ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/24/)), his offer to take Pall into his house to find her a husband ([17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/17/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/20/)), his discussions about Tom’s estate and condolences to his Cozen Scott at the loss of his wife ( [4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/04/)) along with his illness ([14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/14/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/15/), [17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/17/), [19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/19/), [31](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/31/)). Uncle Wight reveals his true intentions as he expresses his desire to father a child with Elizabeth along with the bribe of “500 _l._ money or jewels beforehand, and make[ing] the child his heir”, thus leaving a most disturbed Sam to realize that “all of his kindness is but lust of her” ([11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/11/)).

# June 1664

Tangiers is in the forefront with news of Lord Teviot’s death ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/01/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/15/)); poorly run committee meetings ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/03/), [4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/04/), [10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/10/), [13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/13/)); Sam’s efforts to secure and provision the ships ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/16/), [24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/24/)) and a potential payout from Captain Taylor ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/03/)).

Concerns surround Lord Sandwich as Pepys and Lady Sandwich worry about his debts ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/23/), [29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/29/)). Sam moves to ensure the security of the Wardrobe position once promised to his father ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/04/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/20/)). Sam (and possibly Lady Sandwich) meet Mrs. Becke, the rumored mistress of Lord Sandwich ([14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/14/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/20/)).

Mr. Coventry gives Sam an interesting discourse on active and passive valour ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/04/)) while Mr. Pierce provides contrasts of another sort when he gives Sam a tour of the Queen’s bedchamber and closet and the King’s closet ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/24/)).

# July 1664

Sam argues with Elizabeth about a pair of earring she has bought ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/04/)). The couple reconciles and visits Lord Sandwich aboard the Hope ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/04/)) prior to Elizabeth’s departure to the country ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/09/), [10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/10/), [11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/11/)). Lord Sandwich shares details of his estate with Sam ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/15/)) and warns him of a situation where Sam has inadvertently angered the Lord Chancellor ([14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/14/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/15/), [16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/16/)). Sam tries to resolve the conflict of the cutting of the timber from Clarendon Parke with the help of Sir George Carteret ([18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/18/)), but by month end, Mr. Coventry has placed Sam in a position of divided loyalty on this issue ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/23/)).

Sam records two lists including Dr. Burnett’s health advice ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/01/)) and input about how to have children ([26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/26/)). Sam learns of Mrs. Lane’s marriage ([21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/21/)), but later meets her for a pleasurable tryst ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/23/)). Sam is sworn in for the Committee for Fishing ([7](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/07/), [9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/09/)) and works with Warren on a contract for 1,000 Gottenburg masts ([21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/21/)). By month end he finds himself joyfully over the 1,000 _l._ level and has splurged on seeing two plays, including “Worse and Worse” and “The Bondman”.

# August 1664

Sam decides to secure a female companion for Elizabeth ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/01/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/15/), [23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/23/)) and a boy for himself. By month end Tom Edwards is clothed for the job ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/24/), [27](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/27/)) and Will has brought forth a strong candidate for Elizabeth ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/29/)). Sam designates a room in his home for his “musique room’ and the transformation works begins. Elizabeth’s return home ([7](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/07/)) does not curb Sam’s appetite for a tryst with Mrs. Lane ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/15/)) who is now pregnant and finds her husband in need of a job. Troubles still brew with Tom’s illegitimate child ([25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/25/)).

Sam’s health remains a concern with his bothersome cold legs causing him to have a special coat made for indoors ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/01/), [13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/13/), [14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/14/)). Batten supplies Sam with Epsum water which helps him with his ongoing bowels issues ([17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/17/), [21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/21/)). Sam has a case made for his stone, costing him 24_s._, a large expense for such an item, but a precious reminder of surviving his dangerous operation ([19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/19/), [27](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/27/)).

Sam rationalises his vow against plays ([8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/08/)). Between himself and Elizabeth they see: “Bartholomew’s Fayre” ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/02/)), “The Rivall Ladys” ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/04/)), “Flora’s Figary” ([8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/08/)), “Henry the Fifth” ([8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/08/)) and “The Court Secret” ([18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/18/)). Sam enjoys seeing paintings of the Queen and Frances Stewart ([26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/26/)). For his scientific interests he has his slide rule engraved ([10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/10/), [13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/13/)) and buys a microscope and a scotoscope ([13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/13/)).

# September 1664

The recent arrival of Mary Mercer, Elizabeth’s new gentlewoman, and Tom, Sam’s ‘boy,’ creates a focus on the ‘family’. They enjoy trips to Bartholomew Fayre ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/02/), [7](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/07/)), plays ([10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/10/)), shopping for the home ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/16/)), and a lovely family time where ‘my wife and Mercer and Tom and I sat till eleven at night, singing, fiddling, and a great joy it is to see me master of so much pleasure in my house, that it is and will be still, I hope, a constant pleasure to me to be at home” ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/09/)). Sam spends 10 _l._ on new clothes for Elizabeth, and compliments her new suit of moyre ([5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/05/), [19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/19/)). Elizabeth believes she is with child ([22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/22/)), but by month’s end it’s clear that she is not. While Sam’s jealousy is needlessly piqued by Mr. Pen’s visits to Elizabeth ([5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/05/), [14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/14/)) he still indulges himself with his ladies, including news that Betty Lane wants him to assist her in finding a job for her new husband ([5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/05/)) and his secret trysts with Jane Welsh ([11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/11/), [12](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/12/), [18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/18/), [19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/19/)). The month ends with a disagreement between Sam and Elizabeth over her household accounts ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/29/)).

Sam admits to himself that he has been remiss in his work this month ([17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/17/)) although Mr. Andrew’s victualling contract brings promises of a payment to Sam of 100 _l._ War preparations continue with Prince Rupert readying the Henrietta ([5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/05/), [6](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/06/)) and news of beating the Dutch in Guinny ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/29/)).

[Read the full diary entries for September 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/)

* * *

# October 1664

Sam works on Warren’s timber contract ([18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/18/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/25/)), Mr. Bridge’s calico contract ([8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/08/), [12](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/12/)), the Fishery Committee ([10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/10/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/25/), [29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/29/)) and experiments to test the quality of cordage ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/03/)). As Sam welcomes Lord Sandwich on his return ([17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/17/)), the Dutch tension heats up and Rupert writes of the dangers to his fleet in Portsmouth ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/24/)). Sam and his extended family enjoy seeing the launch of a new ship ([25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/25/)).

Sam visits his parents while in Brampton ([14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/14/)) and his mother begs him to make peace with his brother John ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/15/)). Elizabeth is angered at Sam for “gadding abroad to look after beauties” ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/02/)). This has becoming a more consuming past time to Sam these days with his interactions with Mrs. Lane ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/01/)), the barber’s maid Jane ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/03/)), Mrs. Bagwell ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/03/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/20/)) and an unknown beauty that he follows home from church ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/09/)). Mr Crocker brings Sam a globe of glasse intended to help with Sam’s eyesight ([7](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/07/)).

[Read the full diary entries for October 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/)

* * *

# November 1664

Sam sees Mr. Coventry off to sea with the Duke of York ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/04/), [8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/08/)) and is called before the King’s Cabinet Council and asked questions by the King himself ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/09/)). Sam presents a letter to Sir G. Carteret to show to the King regarding his desire to be a Commissioner of the Prize Office ([22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/22/)) and works with Carteret to prepare a well padded account of the cost of the war ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/23/)) with hopes that the House will supply desperately needed funding. The House approves 2,500,000 _l._ for the Navy over three years.

Sam hears gossip that Lord Sandwich may be sent to be Governor of Tangier ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/03/)). He sees the Book of Heraldry and reads the entries of the Duke of Monmouth and Lord Sandwich ([11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/11/)). Susan becomes sick and Sam fears it is the measles or scarlet fever ([10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/10/), [11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/11/)). Tom also has pains which Dr. Holliard diagnoses as a bladder stone ([22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/22/), [23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/23/)). While Sam comments on Mrs. Lane’s sad state ([25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/25/)) his physical relationship with Mrs. Bagwell ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/03/), [8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/08/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/15/)) escalates.

[Read the full diary entries for November 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/)

* * *

# December 1664

At the start of the month, Sam is pleased that the Duke of York and Mr. Coventry have returned safely from sea ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/03/), [5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/05/)). Other pleasant conversations abound about the great Comet ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/15/)): Sam notes that Lord Sandwich ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/15/)), the King and Queen ([17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/17/)) have seen it, and eventually he sees it for himself ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/24/), [27](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/27/)).

In a rash act of temper, Sam is angered at Elizabeth. He hits her soundly causing a painful and severely blackened eye ([19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/19/)). Elizabeth, still quite bruised, remains housebound throughout the Christmas holiday period ([25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/25/)) and Sam makes up an excuse for her not attending an unusual dinner invitation from the Battens ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/23/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/25/), [26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/26/)). In spite of Sam’s being “vexed at my heart” over what he had done to Elizabeth, it does not stop him from pursuing Mrs. Bagwell. He continues to plot to be with her, finally finding a pleasing “success” when he “invites” himself to their house and then sends her husband away ( [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/15/), [16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/16/), [19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/19/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/20/)).

In regards to finances, Sam has almost fully settled with Tom Trice ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/23/)). He buys himself a looking glass for the dining room ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/16/), [17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/17/)), some books and a silver sugar box, spoons and forks ([14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/14/), [30](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/30/)). A sermon on “duty to parents” ([11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/11/)) seems to have hit home as Sam buys a gift of fruit for his father for Christmas ([14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/14/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/15/)). Sam summarizes his year end status and is pleased to find himself worth 1349 _l._ ([31](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/31/)).
