# Summary of 1664’s diary entries

# January 1664

Sam’s New Year begins with the “bill of exchange” from Deering via Luellin which finds an ebullient Sam 50 _l._ richer, yet still rationalizing the ethics of this and potential future ‘payments’ ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/01/), [5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/05/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/25/)). His New Year happily brings the end to his vow against plays. Sam’s disappointment upon seeing the much touted “Henry VIII” ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/01/)) and “The Usurper” ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/02/)) are followed by a vow to limit the number of plays he will see per month ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/02/)). Not to be at a loss for “entertainment” Sam finds himself highly interested in the case of the stolen jewels of Mr. Tyran, an “old man, a merchant” ([8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/08/)). As the case unfolds, a Colonel Turner is accused, tried and hanged with an estimate of 12-14,000 people, including Sam, attending the execution ([10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/10/), [16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/16/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/20/), [21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/21/)).

Sam’s concern about his relationship with Lord Sandwich continues. He ponders inviting “my Lord” to dinner, but as their exchanges over the month unfold Sam thinks it best to “forbear my laying out my money upon a dinner till I see him in a better posture” ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/09/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/20/)). Where his relationship with Sandwich feels unsure, his relationship with Mrs. Lane becomes more intimate ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/09/), [11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/11/), [16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/16/)). Although his visits to her bring Sam sexual fulfillment they also may be the cause of his growing but unfounded jealousy towards Elizabeth. His jealous concerns over Will and Pembleton ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/09/), [17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/17/), [18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/18/), [28](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/28/)) leave Sam to confess his irrational fears: “God knows I have no reason to do so, or to expect her being so true to me as I would have to her ([18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/18/)). By month end he does follow through on his promise to Elizabeth and finishes his will ([20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/20/), [23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/23/), [24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/24/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/25/), [28](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/28/), [30](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/30/)). While Sam’s jealousy reigns against the younger men in Elizabeth’s life Sam can only think good of Uncle Wight who seems mysteriously and overly interested to know if Elizabeth is with child. Sam hopefully believes that Uncle Wight intends to leave something to them in his will ([12](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/12/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/15/), [21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/21/)). In other family matters, brother Tom’s health seems to have taken a turn for the worse, with worries that he is in a deep consumption ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/09/), [10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/10/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/20/)).

In the Royal circles Sam watches the King’s tennis match noting his disgust at the false flattery given the monarch “but to see how the King’s play was extolled without any cause at all, was a loathsome sight, though sometimes, indeed, he did play very well and deserved to be commended; but such open flattery is beastly” ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/04/)). Sam is likewise unimpressed by the King’s lewd response to a Quaker girl who has brought forth a warrant ([11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/11/)). Mr. Pierce tells Sam the seedy gossip that Lady Castlemaine is “out” as the King now dallies openly with Frances Stuart and that the Duke of Monmouth is treated like a “Prince of the Blood”. Mr. Pierce shares the flattering opinion that the Duke of York “do give himself up to business, and is like to prove a noble Prince” to which Sam heartily agrees that “I do from my heart think he will” ([20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/20/)).

[Read the full diary entries for January 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/01/)

* * *

# February 1664

Talk of the growing tension between the English and the Dutch circulates ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/02/), [9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/09/)) with the Dutch proclaiming that they are the “Soveraigne of all the South Seas” ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/15/)). Business concerns include issues regarding the quality of masts ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/16/), [17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/17/), [18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/18/), [21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/21/), [22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/22/)); a letter on the behalf of Mr. Barrow ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/16/)); Mr. Maes’ customs issue ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/04/), [10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/10/)); hempe and trade ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/24/)); Creed and his pieces of eight ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/04/), [10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/10/)); a review of Lord Peterborough’s accounts ([13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/13/), [18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/18/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/25/), [26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/26/), [27](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/27/)) and a detailed report on the state of England’s Revenues by Sir Phillip Warwick, which totally captivates Sam ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/29/)). Sam benefits from his position through a gifts from Sir W. Warren ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/02/)), Mr. Falconer ([11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/11/)), and Mrs. Russell.

Elizabeth brings news that Balty and his wife will leave for his soldier duty in Holland ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/03/)). Uncle Wright’s “caresses” and private visits to Elizabeth leave Sam to believe that “it looks strange putting all together, but yet I am in hopes he means well” ([19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/19/), [22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/22/), [26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/26/)). The concerns that Sam had early in the month that he may have gotten Mrs. Lane pregnant ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/01/)) were not put at ease when the marriage that he was hoping to arrange between her and Hawley seems to fall apart ([8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/08/)). Sam vows that he is now “resolved wholly to avoid occasion of further ill with her” ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/29/)). His receives advice from Mr. Howe regarding his relationship with Lord Sandwich ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/03/), [8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/08/)). Howe “did of himself advise me to appear more free with my Lord and to come to him, for my own strangeness he tells me he thinks do make my Lord the worse.” ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/29/))

Court gossip includes the Duke’s new perriwigg ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/15/)), Lady Castlemaine’s theater antics ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/01/)), the scathing condition of foreign policy, pathetic internal court politics, and a deep concern for the overall welfare of England under King Charles II ([22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/22/)). On a more playful note, Sam enjoys seeing “The Indian Queene” with Elizabeth ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/01/)), buying two books ([22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/22/)), observing sand, louse and mites under a microscope ([13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/13/)), watching marble being cut ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/24/)) and receiving a new mastiffe named “Towser” ([17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/17/)) who he thinks he will give to his father as a present ([18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/02/18/)).

# March 1664

March begins on an upbeat note as Lord Sandwich praises Sam to Lord Peterborough and Povy ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/03/)). Lord Sandwich’s favour also yields Sam’s a role as an assistant under the Duke of York in the newly created Corporation of the Royal Fishery ([10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/10/)). Sam celebrates the new month by bending his vows to see two plays, “The Unfortunate Lovers” and “Heraclius” ([7](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/07/), [8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/08/)).

Happiness is short lived when Tom takes a turn for the worse. When Mrs. Turner’s son arrives with a note that Tom’s illness may be the pox ([13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/13/)), Sam is rightly upset regarding such shameful accusations. Sam visits Tom several times over the following days as his health deteriorates. Sam assists as two different doctors check Tom’s body for signs of the pox, but there are none, which offer Sam some relief ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/15/)). Meanwhile Sam starts to gather details regarding the nature of Tom’s lifestyle, including his debts, mysterious meetings with Cave and Cranburne, and his bad husbandry ([13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/13/), [14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/14/)). Tom passes away, and amidst funeral preparations, Sam discovers among Tom’s papers some back-stabbing letters written about him by his brother John ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/15/)). Sam’s father arrives a “poor man, very sad and sickly,” and has barely a moment to grieve before an angry Sam confronts him about the content of John’s letters ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/16/), [18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/18/), [19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/19/), [21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/21/)). As the days progress, Sam seeks advice from Mr. Moore regarding who should administer Tom’s estate ([27](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/27/)).

Among the despair, a hilarious lightness is found when Sam decides that Mrs. Buggin’s decidedly beautiful dog should mate with his bitch and he helps him along ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/23/), [24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/24/)). The month ends at Sam’s house with a happy dinner gathering as Sam celebrates his “solemn feast” for the cutting of his stone ([26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/03/26/)).

# April 1664

April brings continued efforts to settle brother Tom’s estate ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/16/)) and the shocking surprise that Tom had fathered a daughter with his maid Margaret ([6](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/06/)). Concerns over a potential Dutch war overwhelm many of Sam’s conversations ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/04/), [13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/13/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/20/), [23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/23/)). While Howe and others plot for a favored spot should war begin ([12](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/12/)), Sam’s fears for the safety of his accounts, which could be lost, should Lord Sandwich perish in battle ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/23/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/25/), [26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/26/)). The month ends with a more impending concern over loss of life when Lady Sandwich, Sam’s favourite, becomes ill with either the measles or, as Sam fears, perhaps smallpox ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/29/), [30](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/04/30/)).

# May 1664

Navy work includes Sam’s ongoing disgust with Sir W. Batten ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/03/), [5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/05/), [22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/22/), [26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/26/)); discussions of the possibility of a Dutch War with Coventry ([12](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/12/), [18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/18/), [21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/21/), [22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/22/), [29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/29/)); his bribe from Captain Taylor ([27](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/27/)); his interest in shipbuilding ([7](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/07/), [13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/13/), [30](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/30/)); and his unusual role as a go-between to elicit Lord Sandwich (at Coventry’s request) to see if he would go to sea under the Duke of York should war with the Dutch prevail ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/29/),31).

In personal matters Sam is relieved to find Lady Sandwich on the mend ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/09/), [12](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/12/)) and thrilled that work on his closet was done so well ([6](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/06/)). On the more worrisome side, he notes the death of Uncle Fenner ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/24/)), his offer to take Pall into his house to find her a husband ([17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/17/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/20/)), his discussions about Tom’s estate and condolences to his Cozen Scott at the loss of his wife ( [4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/04/)) along with his illness ([14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/14/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/15/), [17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/17/), [19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/19/), [31](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/31/)). Uncle Wight reveals his true intentions as he expresses his desire to father a child with Elizabeth along with the bribe of “500 _l._ money or jewels beforehand, and make[ing] the child his heir”, thus leaving a most disturbed Sam to realize that “all of his kindness is but lust of her” ([11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/05/11/)).

# June 1664

Tangiers is in the forefront with news of Lord Teviot’s death ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/01/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/15/)); poorly run committee meetings ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/03/), [4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/04/), [10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/10/), [13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/13/)); Sam’s efforts to secure and provision the ships ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/16/), [24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/24/)) and a potential payout from Captain Taylor ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/03/)).

Concerns surround Lord Sandwich as Pepys and Lady Sandwich worry about his debts ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/23/), [29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/29/)). Sam moves to ensure the security of the Wardrobe position once promised to his father ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/04/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/20/)). Sam (and possibly Lady Sandwich) meet Mrs. Becke, the rumored mistress of Lord Sandwich ([14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/14/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/20/)).

Mr. Coventry gives Sam an interesting discourse on active and passive valour ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/04/)) while Mr. Pierce provides contrasts of another sort when he gives Sam a tour of the Queen’s bedchamber and closet and the King’s closet ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/06/24/)).

# July 1664

Sam argues with Elizabeth about a pair of earring she has bought ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/04/)). The couple reconciles and visits Lord Sandwich aboard the Hope ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/04/)) prior to Elizabeth’s departure to the country ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/09/), [10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/10/), [11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/11/)). Lord Sandwich shares details of his estate with Sam ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/15/)) and warns him of a situation where Sam has inadvertently angered the Lord Chancellor ([14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/14/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/15/), [16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/16/)). Sam tries to resolve the conflict of the cutting of the timber from Clarendon Parke with the help of Sir George Carteret ([18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/18/)), but by month end, Mr. Coventry has placed Sam in a position of divided loyalty on this issue ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/23/)).

Sam records two lists including Dr. Burnett’s health advice ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/01/)) and input about how to have children ([26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/26/)). Sam learns of Mrs. Lane’s marriage ([21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/21/)), but later meets her for a pleasurable tryst ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/23/)). Sam is sworn in for the Committee for Fishing ([7](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/07/), [9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/09/)) and works with Warren on a contract for 1,000 Gottenburg masts ([21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/07/21/)). By month end he finds himself joyfully over the 1,000 _l._ level and has splurged on seeing two plays, including “Worse and Worse” and “The Bondman”.

# August 1664

Sam decides to secure a female companion for Elizabeth ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/01/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/15/), [23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/23/)) and a boy for himself. By month end Tom Edwards is clothed for the job ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/24/), [27](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/27/)) and Will has brought forth a strong candidate for Elizabeth ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/29/)). Sam designates a room in his home for his “musique room’ and the transformation works begins. Elizabeth’s return home ([7](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/07/)) does not curb Sam’s appetite for a tryst with Mrs. Lane ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/15/)) who is now pregnant and finds her husband in need of a job. Troubles still brew with Tom’s illegitimate child ([25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/25/)).

Sam’s health remains a concern with his bothersome cold legs causing him to have a special coat made for indoors ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/01/), [13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/13/), [14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/14/)). Batten supplies Sam with Epsum water which helps him with his ongoing bowels issues ([17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/17/), [21](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/21/)). Sam has a case made for his stone, costing him 24_s._, a large expense for such an item, but a precious reminder of surviving his dangerous operation ([19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/19/), [27](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/27/)).

Sam rationalises his vow against plays ([8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/08/)). Between himself and Elizabeth they see: “Bartholomew’s Fayre” ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/02/)), “The Rivall Ladys” ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/04/)), “Flora’s Figary” ([8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/08/)), “Henry the Fifth” ([8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/08/)) and “The Court Secret” ([18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/18/)). Sam enjoys seeing paintings of the Queen and Frances Stewart ([26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/26/)). For his scientific interests he has his slide rule engraved ([10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/10/), [13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/13/)) and buys a microscope and a scotoscope ([13](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/08/13/)).

# September 1664

The recent arrival of Mary Mercer, Elizabeth’s new gentlewoman, and Tom, Sam’s ‘boy,’ creates a focus on the ‘family’. They enjoy trips to Bartholomew Fayre ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/02/), [7](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/07/)), plays ([10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/10/)), shopping for the home ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/16/)), and a lovely family time where ‘my wife and Mercer and Tom and I sat till eleven at night, singing, fiddling, and a great joy it is to see me master of so much pleasure in my house, that it is and will be still, I hope, a constant pleasure to me to be at home” ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/09/)). Sam spends 10 _l._ on new clothes for Elizabeth, and compliments her new suit of moyre ([5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/05/), [19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/19/)). Elizabeth believes she is with child ([22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/22/)), but by month’s end it’s clear that she is not. While Sam’s jealousy is needlessly piqued by Mr. Pen’s visits to Elizabeth ([5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/05/), [14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/14/)) he still indulges himself with his ladies, including news that Betty Lane wants him to assist her in finding a job for her new husband ([5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/05/)) and his secret trysts with Jane Welsh ([11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/11/), [12](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/12/), [18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/18/), [19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/19/)). The month ends with a disagreement between Sam and Elizabeth over her household accounts ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/29/)).

Sam admits to himself that he has been remiss in his work this month ([17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/17/)) although Mr. Andrew’s victualling contract brings promises of a payment to Sam of 100 _l._ War preparations continue with Prince Rupert readying the Henrietta ([5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/05/), [6](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/06/)) and news of beating the Dutch in Guinny ([29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/09/29/)).

# October 1664

Sam works on Warren’s timber contract ([18](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/18/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/25/)), Mr. Bridge’s calico contract ([8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/08/), [12](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/12/)), the Fishery Committee ([10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/10/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/25/), [29](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/29/)) and experiments to test the quality of cordage ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/03/)). As Sam welcomes Lord Sandwich on his return ([17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/17/)), the Dutch tension heats up and Rupert writes of the dangers to his fleet in Portsmouth ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/24/)). Sam and his extended family enjoy seeing the launch of a new ship ([25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/25/)).

Sam visits his parents while in Brampton ([14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/14/)) and his mother begs him to make peace with his brother John ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/15/)). Elizabeth is angered at Sam for “gadding abroad to look after beauties” ([2](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/02/)). This has becoming a more consuming past time to Sam these days with his interactions with Mrs. Lane ([1](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/01/)), the barber’s maid Jane ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/03/)), Mrs. Bagwell ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/03/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/20/)) and an unknown beauty that he follows home from church ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/09/)). Mr Crocker brings Sam a globe of glasse intended to help with Sam’s eyesight ([7](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/10/07/)).

# November 1664

Sam sees Mr. Coventry off to sea with the Duke of York ([4](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/04/), [8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/08/)) and is called before the King’s Cabinet Council and asked questions by the King himself ([9](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/09/)). Sam presents a letter to Sir G. Carteret to show to the King regarding his desire to be a Commissioner of the Prize Office ([22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/22/)) and works with Carteret to prepare a well padded account of the cost of the war ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/23/)) with hopes that the House will supply desperately needed funding. The House approves 2,500,000 _l._ for the Navy over three years.

Sam hears gossip that Lord Sandwich may be sent to be Governor of Tangier ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/03/)). He sees the Book of Heraldry and reads the entries of the Duke of Monmouth and Lord Sandwich ([11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/11/)). Susan becomes sick and Sam fears it is the measles or scarlet fever ([10](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/10/), [11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/11/)). Tom also has pains which Dr. Holliard diagnoses as a bladder stone ([22](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/22/), [23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/23/)). While Sam comments on Mrs. Lane’s sad state ([25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/25/)) his physical relationship with Mrs. Bagwell ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/03/), [8](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/08/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/11/15/)) escalates.

# December 1664

At the start of the month, Sam is pleased that the Duke of York and Mr. Coventry have returned safely from sea ([3](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/03/), [5](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/05/)). Other pleasant conversations abound about the great Comet ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/15/)): Sam notes that Lord Sandwich ([15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/15/)), the King and Queen ([17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/17/)) have seen it, and eventually he sees it for himself ([24](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/24/), [27](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/27/)).

In a rash act of temper, Sam is angered at Elizabeth. He hits her soundly causing a painful and severely blackened eye ([19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/19/)). Elizabeth, still quite bruised, remains housebound throughout the Christmas holiday period ([25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/25/)) and Sam makes up an excuse for her not attending an unusual dinner invitation from the Battens ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/23/), [25](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/25/), [26](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/26/)). In spite of Sam’s being “vexed at my heart” over what he had done to Elizabeth, it does not stop him from pursuing Mrs. Bagwell. He continues to plot to be with her, finally finding a pleasing “success” when he “invites” himself to their house and then sends her husband away ( [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/15/), [16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/16/), [19](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/19/), [20](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/20/)).

In regards to finances, Sam has almost fully settled with Tom Trice ([23](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/23/)). He buys himself a looking glass for the dining room ([16](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/16/), [17](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/17/)), some books and a silver sugar box, spoons and forks ([14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/14/), [30](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/30/)). A sermon on “duty to parents” ([11](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/11/)) seems to have hit home as Sam buys a gift of fruit for his father for Christmas ([14](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/14/), [15](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/15/)). Sam summarizes his year end status and is pleased to find himself worth 1349 _l._ ([31](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/31/)).

# Sunday 1 December 1661

(Lord’s day). In the morning at [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/) and heard [Mr. Mills](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1215/). At [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) dined and with me by appointment [Mr. Sanchy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2890/), who should have brought his mistress, [Mrs. Mary Archer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3326/), of [Cambridge](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2589/), but she could not come, but we had a good dinner for him. And so in the afternoon [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) went to church, and he and I stayed at home and drank and talked, and he stayed with me till night and supped with me, when I expected to have seen [Jack Cole](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/735/) and [Lem. Wagstaffe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3341/), but they did not come.

We this day cut a brave collar of [brawn](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1862/) from [Winchcombe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11617/) which proves very good, and also opened the glass of [girkins](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3342/) which [Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/) did give my wife the other day, which are rare things.

So at night to bed.

There hath lately been great clapping up of some old statesmen, such as [Ireton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3343/), [Moyer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3344/), and others, and they say, upon a great plot, but I believe no such thing; but it is but justice that they should be served as they served the poor [Cavaliers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/698/); and I believe it will oftentimes be so as long as I live, whether there be cause or no.

### Maurie Beck on 3 Dec 2004•Link

One hypothesis holds that pathogens mutate to more virulent form only when they have the chance to spread before killing off the means of transmission.

There is always mutation. Most mutations are neutral or deleterious, but some are beneficial. Virulence seems to be associated with the mode of transmission. For example, pathogens that are water-borne or transmitted through a vector (e.g. insects) are generally more virulent than from person to person. The coming plague is transmitted by a flea from the primary host (rats) to humans. In this case, virulence is favored, even if it means the death of the human host. A very sick human host is more likely to be bitten by a flea which passes on the bacteria to new hosts than a less sick host with a less virulent form.

### [Terry Foreman](https://www.pepysdiary.com/account/profile/41/ "See more about this person")on 1 Nov 2017•Link

"There hath lately been great clapping up of some old statesmen, such as Ireton, Moyer, and others, and they say, upon a great plot"

The was the Yarrenton or Baxter or Pakington Plot. John Ireton had been Lord Mayor in 1658-9, and Samuel Moyer a member of Cromwell's Council of State. The government claimed to have prevented an uprising and to have uncovered a most important rebel organization. (L&M) In November 1661 Sir John Pakington informed Sir Edward Nicholas of the discovery of a supposed presbyterian plot in his neighbourhood, and forwarded him some intercepted letters which had been brought to hiin. Several ministers, Baxter among the number, were implicated, and arrests were made. The letters were probably forgeries, and the charges were never proved. Andrew Yarrenton, who wrote an account of the affair in 1681, regarded Pakington as the inventor of the plot (which frequently went by his name) and the writer of the letters. Pakington was the intimate friend of Bishop Morlev [see Morley, Gkorge] and of Sir Ralph Clare, and thus came into collision with Richard Baxter. Baxter accused Pakington of having intercepted a letter of his, which proved to be of a purely private nature, and of sending it to London. [books.google.com/books?pg=PA90&lp…](https://books.google.com/books?pg=PA90&lpg=PA90&dq=Pakington%27s+plot+1661&sig=Xegil2U608la9dfmjBL3fHjpXIg&id=Jc4cAQAAIAAJ&ots=rsWWDYRLl5&output=text) Cf. Pepys's scepticism at 30 October 1661. He was himself to suffer similarly as a victim of the Popish Plot on 1679. (L&M note)

# Sunday 1 December 1661

(Lord’s day). In the morning at [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/) and heard [Mr. Mills](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1215/). At [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) dined and with me by appointment [Mr. Sanchy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2890/), who should have brought his mistress, [Mrs. Mary Archer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3326/), of [Cambridge](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2589/), but she could not come, but we had a good dinner for him. And so in the afternoon [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) went to church, and he and I stayed at home and drank and talked, and he stayed with me till night and supped with me, when I expected to have seen [Jack Cole](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/735/) and [Lem. Wagstaffe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3341/), but they did not come.

We this day cut a brave collar of [brawn](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1862/) from [Winchcombe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11617/) which proves very good, and also opened the glass of [girkins](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3342/) which [Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/) did give my wife the other day, which are rare things.

So at night to bed.

There hath lately been great clapping up of some old statesmen, such as [Ireton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3343/), [Moyer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3344/), and others, and they say, upon a great plot, but I believe no such thing; but it is but justice that they should be served as they served the poor [Cavaliers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/698/); and I believe it will oftentimes be so as long as I live, whether there be cause or no.

This evening my brother [Tom](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/236/) was with me, and I did talk again to him about [Mr. Townsend’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/947/) daughter, and I do intend to put the business in hand. I pray God give a good end to it.

One hypothesis holds that pathogens mutate to more virulent form only when they have the chance to spread before killing off the means of transmission.

There is always mutation. Most mutations are neutral or deleterious, but some are beneficial. Virulence seems to be associated with the mode of transmission. For example, pathogens that are water-borne or transmitted through a vector (e.g. insects) are generally more virulent than from person to person. The coming plague is transmitted by a flea from the primary host (rats) to humans. In this case, virulence is favored, even if it means the death of the human host. A very sick human host is more likely to be bitten by a flea which passes on the bacteria to new hosts than a less sick host with a less virulent form.

### [Terry Foreman](https://www.pepysdiary.com/account/profile/41/ "See more about this person")on 1 Nov 2017•Link

"There hath lately been great clapping up of some old statesmen, such as Ireton, Moyer, and others, and they say, upon a great plot"

The was the Yarrenton or Baxter or Pakington Plot. John Ireton had been Lord Mayor in 1658-9, and Samuel Moyer a member of Cromwell's Council of State. The government claimed to have prevented an uprising and to have uncovered a most important rebel organization. (L&M) In November 1661 Sir John Pakington informed Sir Edward Nicholas of the discovery of a supposed presbyterian plot in his neighbourhood, and forwarded him some intercepted letters which had been brought to hiin. Several ministers, Baxter among the number, were implicated, and arrests were made. The letters were probably forgeries, and the charges were never proved. Andrew Yarrenton, who wrote an account of the affair in 1681, regarded Pakington as the inventor of the plot (which frequently went by his name) and the writer of the letters. Pakington was the intimate friend of Bishop Morlev [see Morley, Gkorge] and of Sir Ralph Clare, and thus came into collision with Richard Baxter. Baxter accused Pakington of having intercepted a letter of his, which proved to be of a purely private nature, and of sending it to London. [books.google.com/books?pg=PA90&lp…](https://books.google.com/books?pg=PA90&lpg=PA90&dq=Pakington%27s+plot+1661&sig=Xegil2U608la9dfmjBL3fHjpXIg&id=Jc4cAQAAIAAJ&ots=rsWWDYRLl5&output=text) Cf. Pepys's scepticism at 30 October 1661. He was himself to suffer similarly as a victim of the Popish Plot on 1679. (L&M note)

# Monday 1 December 1662

Up and by coach with [Sir John Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) and [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) to [the Duke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) chamber, where, as is usual, my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) and all of us, after his being ready, to his closett, and there discoursed of matters of the Navy, and here [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) did do me the great kindness to take notice to the Duke of my pains in making a collection of all contracts about [masts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5619/), which have been of great use to us. Thence I to my Lord Sandwich’s, to [Mr. Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/340/), to talk a little about business; and then over [the Parke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/248/) (where I first in my life, it being a great frost, did see people sliding with their [skeates](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5690/), which is a very pretty art), to Mr. Coventry’s chamber to [St. James’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/466/), where we all met to a [venison pasty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/384/), and were very merry, [Major Norwood](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/678/) being with us, whom they did play upon for his surrendering of [Dunkirk](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/607/).

Here we staid till three or four o’clock; and so to the Council Chamber, where there met the Duke of York, [Prince Rupert](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1357/), [Duke of Albemarle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/), my Lord Sandwich, [Sir Wm. Compton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/751/), Mr. Coventry, Sir J. Minnes, [Sir R. Ford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1347/), [Sir W. Rider](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1766/), myself, and [Captain Cuttance](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/583/), as [Commissioners for Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5243/). And after our Commission was read by [Mr. Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/), who I perceive is to be our Secretary, we did fall to discourse of matters: as, first, the supplying them forthwith with victualls; then the reducing it to make way for the money, which upon their reduction is to go to the building of the [Mole](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5384/); and so to other matters, ordered as against next meeting.

This done we broke up, and I to [the Cockpitt](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/179/), with much crowding and waiting, where I saw [“The Valiant Cidd”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5691/) —[Translated from the “Cid” of Corneille]— acted, a play I have read with great delight, but is a most dull thing acted, which I never understood before, there being no pleasure in it, though done by [Betterton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2307/) and by [Ianthe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4034/), And [another fine wench](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5692/) that is come in the room of Roxalana nor did [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) or [queen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) once smile all the whole play, nor any of the company seem to take any pleasure but what was in the greatness and gallantry of the company.

Thence to my Lord’s, and Mr. Moore being in bed I staid not, but with a [link](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1167/) walked [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) and got thither by 12 o’clock, knocked up [my boy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1248/), and put myself to bed.

### Paul Dyson on 2 Dec 2005•Link

“knocked up my boy” — but he’s just saying he woke his boy up by knocking the door, so he’d let Sam in.  
Knock up is a long-lasting phrase, but it's modern slang meaning is fairly recent. In industrial areas where people needed to rise early to get to their morning shift, they used to employ a "knocker-up" who roused the workers by rattling on the front upstairs window, using perhaps an old fishing rod with an umbrella rib attached, and waiting for an answering call or signal. This practice was certainly alive and well in the Lancashire cotton towns in the 1920s and probably later until cheap alarm clocks became common. The knocker-up received a fee, say a penny (old currency) per house per week. But who knocked up the knocker-up?

# Monday 1 December 1662

Up and by coach with [Sir John Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) and [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) to [the Duke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) chamber, where, as is usual, my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) and all of us, after his being ready, to his closett, and there discoursed of matters of the Navy, and here [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) did do me the great kindness to take notice to the Duke of my pains in making a collection of all contracts about [masts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5619/), which have been of great use to us. Thence I to my Lord Sandwich’s, to [Mr. Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/340/), to talk a little about business; and then over [the Parke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/248/) (where I first in my life, it being a great frost, did see people sliding with their [skeates](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5690/), which is a very pretty art), to Mr. Coventry’s chamber to [St. James’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/466/), where we all met to a [venison pasty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/384/), and were very merry, [Major Norwood](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/678/) being with us, whom they did play upon for his surrendering of [Dunkirk](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/607/).

Here we staid till three or four o’clock; and so to the Council Chamber, where there met the Duke of York, [Prince Rupert](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1357/), [Duke of Albemarle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/), my Lord Sandwich, [Sir Wm. Compton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/751/), Mr. Coventry, Sir J. Minnes, [Sir R. Ford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1347/), [Sir W. Rider](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1766/), myself, and [Captain Cuttance](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/583/), as [Commissioners for Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5243/). And after our Commission was read by [Mr. Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/), who I perceive is to be our Secretary, we did fall to discourse of matters: as, first, the supplying them forthwith with victualls; then the reducing it to make way for the money, which upon their reduction is to go to the building of the [Mole](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5384/); and so to other matters, ordered as against next meeting.

This done we broke up, and I to [the Cockpitt](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/179/), with much crowding and waiting, where I saw [“The Valiant Cidd”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5691/) —[Translated from the “Cid” of Corneille]— acted, a play I have read with great delight, but is a most dull thing acted, which I never understood before, there being no pleasure in it, though done by [Betterton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2307/) and by [Ianthe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4034/), And [another fine wench](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5692/) that is come in the room of Roxalana nor did [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) or [queen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) once smile all the whole play, nor any of the company seem to take any pleasure but what was in the greatness and gallantry of the company.

Thence to my Lord’s, and Mr. Moore being in bed I staid not, but with a [link](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1167/) walked [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) and got thither by 12 o’clock, knocked up [my boy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1248/), and put myself to bed.

“knocked up my boy” — but he’s just saying he woke his boy up by knocking the door, so he’d let Sam in.  
Knock up is a long-lasting phrase, but it's modern slang meaning is fairly recent. In industrial areas where people needed to rise early to get to their morning shift, they used to employ a "knocker-up" who roused the workers by rattling on the front upstairs window, using perhaps an old fishing rod with an umbrella rib attached, and waiting for an answering call or signal. This practice was certainly alive and well in the Lancashire cotton towns in the 1920s and probably later until cheap alarm clocks became common. The knocker-up received a fee, say a penny (old currency) per house per week. But who knocked up the knocker-up?

# Diary entries from December 1666

# [Saturday 1 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/01/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning. At [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and then abroad walking to the [Old Swan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4002/), and in my way I did see a cellar in [Tower Streete](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1117/) in a very fresh fire, the late great winds having blown it up.1 It seemed to be only of log-wood, that Hath kept [the fire](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10319/) all this while in it. Going further, I met my late [Lord Mayor Bludworth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5187/), under whom [the City](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/275/) was burned, and went with him by water to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/). But, Lord! the silly talk that this fellow had, only how ready he would be to part with all his estate in these difficult times to advance [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) service, and complaining that now, as every body did lately in the fire, every body endeavours to save himself, and let the whole perish: but a very weak man he seems to be. I left him at White Hall, he giving 6 _d._ towards the boat, and I to [Westminster Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), where I was again defeated in my expectation of [Burroughs](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8607/). However, I was not much sorry for it, but by coach [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), in the evening, calling at [Faythorne’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/907/), buying three of my [Lady Castlemayne’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1062/) heads, printed this day, which indeed is, as to the head, I think, a very fine picture, and like her. I did this afternoon get [Mrs. Michell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1101/) to let me only have a sight of a pamphlet lately printed, but suppressed and much called after, called [“The Catholique’s Apology;”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10595/) lamenting the severity of the [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) against them, and comparing it with the lenity of other princes to [Protestants](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7980/); giving old and late instances of their loyalty to their princes, whatever is objected against them; and excusing their disquiets in [Queen Elizabeth’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5307/) time, for that it was impossible for them to think her a lawfull Queen, if [Queen Mary](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10596/), who had been owned as such, were so; one being the daughter of the true, and the other of a false wife: and that of the [Gunpowder Treason](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/313/), by saying that it was only the practice of some of us, if not the King, to trepan some of their religion into it, it never being defended by the generality of their Church, nor indeed known by them; and ends with a large Catalogue, in red letters, of the [Catholiques](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/306/) which have lost their lives in the quarrel of the [late King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/624/) and this. The thing is very well writ indeed. So home to my letters, and then to my supper and to bed.

1.   The fire continued burning in some cellars of the ruins of the city for four months, though it rained in the month of October ten days without ceasing (Rugge’s “Diurnal”). — B. ↩

# [Sunday 2 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/02/)

(Lord’s day). Up, and to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), and after church [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, where I met [Betty Michell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5329/) and her [husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9771/), very merry at dinner, and after dinner, having borrowed [Sir W. Pen’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) coach, we to Westminster, they two and [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I to [Mr. Martin’s](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7729/), where find the company almost all come to the christening of [Mrs. Martin’s](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1157/)[child](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10567/), a girl. A great deal of good plain company. After sitting long, till the church was done, the Parson comes, and then we to christen the child. I was Godfather, and [Mrs. Holder](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6677/) ([her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2187/), a good man, I know well), and a pretty lady, that waits, it seems, on my [Lady Bath](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14063/), at [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), her name, [Mrs. Noble](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10598/), were Godmothers. After the christening comes in the [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/) and the [sweetmeats](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4140/), and then to prate and tattle, and then very good company they were, and I among them. Here was old [Mrs. Michell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1101/) and [Howlett](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3065/), and several married women of [the Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), whom I knew mayds. Here was also [Mrs. Burroughs](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8607/) and [Mrs. Bales](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7603/), the young widow, whom I led home, and having staid till the moon was up, I took my pretty gossip to White Hall with us, and I saw her in her lodging, and then my owne company again took coach, and no sooner in the coach but something broke, that we were fain there to stay till a smith could be fetched, which was above an hour, and then it costing me 6 _s._ to mend. Away round by the wall and [Cow Lane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10599/), for fear it should break again; and in pain about the coach all the way. But to ease myself therein Betty Michell did sit at the same end with me … [and there con su mano under my manteau, I did pull off her cheirotheca and did tocar mi cosa con su mano through my chemise, but yet so as to hazer me hazer la grande cosa — and she did let me hazerle sin mucho trabaho. – L&M] Being very much pleased with this, we at last come home, and so to supper, and then sent them by boat home, and we to bed.

When I come home I went to [Sir W. Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/), and there I hear more ill newes still: that all our New England fleete, which went out lately, are put back a third time by foul weather, and dispersed, some to one port and some to another; and their convoys also to [Plymouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5849/); and whether any of them be lost or not, we do not know. This, added to all the rest, do lay us flat in our hopes and courages, every body prophesying destruction to the nation.

# [Monday 3 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/03/)

Up, and, among a great many people that come to speak with me, one was my [Lord Peterborough’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3178/) gentleman, who comes to me to dun me to get some money advanced for my Lord; and I demanding what newes, he tells me that at Court they begin to fear the business of Scotland more and more; and that the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) intends to go to the North to raise an army, and that [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) would have some of the Nobility and others to go and assist; but they were so served the last year, among others his Lord, in raising forces at their own charge, for fear of the French invading us, that they will not be got out now, without money advanced to them by the King, and this is like to be the King’s case for certain, if ever he comes to have need of any army.

He and others gone, I by water to Westminster, and there to the [Exchequer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/242/), and put my [tallys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8499/) in a way of doing for the last quarter. But my not following it the last week has occasioned the clerks some trouble, which I am sorry for, and they are mad at. Thence at noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there find [Kate Joyce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1105/), who dined with me: [Her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1107/) and she are weary of their new life of being an Innkeeper, and will leave it, and would fain get some office; but I know none the foole is fit for, but would be glad to help them, if I could, though they have enough to live on, God be thanked! though their loss hath been to the value of 3000 _l._[W. Joyce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1090/) now has all the trade, she says, the trade being come to that end of the towne. She dined with me, [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) being ill of her months in bed. I left her with my wife, and away myself to [Westminster Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/) by appointment and there found out [Burroughs](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8607/), and I took her by coach as far as the [Lord Treasurer’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4111/) and called at the cake house by [Hales’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2206/), and there in the coach eat and drank and then carried her home … [with much ado making her to tocar mi cosa, she being endeed very averse a alguna cosa of that kind. – L&M] So having set her down in the palace I to the [Swan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1707/), and there did the first time ‘baiser’ the little [sister](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10614/) of [Sarah](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8177/) that is come into her place, and so away by coach home, where to my [vyall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/461/) and supper and then to bed, being weary of the following of my pleasure and sorry for my omitting (though with a true salvo to my vowes) the stating my last month’s accounts in time, as I should, but resolve to settle, and clear all my business before me this month, that I may begin afresh the next yeare, and enjoy some little pleasure freely at [Christmasse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/). So to bed, and with more cheerfulness than I have done a good while, to hear that for certain the Scott rebells are all routed; they having been so bold as to come within three miles of [Edinburgh](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10615/), and there given two or three repulses to the King’s forces, but at last were mastered. Three or four hundred killed or taken, among which their leader, one [Wallis](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10616/), and seven ministers, they having all taken the Covenant a few days before, and sworn to live and die in it, as they did; and so all is likely to be there quiet again. There is also the very good newes come of four New-England ships come home safe to [Falmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10617/) with [masts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5619/) for the King; which is a blessing mighty unexpected, and without which, if for nothing else, we must have failed the next year. But God be praised for thus much good fortune, and send us the continuance of his favour in other things! So to bed.

# [Tuesday 4 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/04/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning. At noon dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/). After dinner presently to my office, and there late and then home to even my Journall and accounts, and then to supper much eased in mind, and last night’s good news, which is more and more confirmed with particulars to very good purpose, and so to bed.

# [Wednesday 5 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/05/)

Up, and by water to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), where we did much business before the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/), which being done, I away [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) by water again, and there to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) till noon busy. At noon home, and [Goodgroome](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2745/) dined with us, who teaches [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) to sing. After dinner I did give him my song, [“Beauty retire,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9571/) which he has often desired of me, and without flattery I think is a very good song. He gone, I to the office, and there late, very busy doing much business, and then home to supper and talk, and then scold with my wife for not reckoning well the times that her musique master hath been with her, but setting down more than I am sure, and did convince her, they had been with her, and in an ill humour of anger with her to bed.

# [Thursday 6 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/06/)

Up, but very good friends with [her](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) before I rose, and so to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the forenoon, and then [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, where [Harman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6860/) dined with us, and great sport to hear him tell how [Will Joyce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1090/) grows rich by the custom of [the City](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/275/) coming to his end of the towne, and how he rants over [his brother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1107/) and [sister](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1105/) for their keeping an Inne, and goes thither and tears like a prince, calling him hosteller and his sister hostess. Then after dinner, my wife and [brother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/117/), in another habit; go out to see a play; but I am not to take notice that I know of my brother’s going. So I to the office, where very busy till late at night, and then home. My wife not pleased with the play, but thinks that it is because she is grown more critical than she used to be, but my brother she says is mighty taken with it. So to supper and to bed.

This day, in [the Gazette](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9931/), is the whole story of defeating the Scotch rebells, and of the creation of the [Duke of Cambridge](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6506/), Knight of the Garter.

# [Friday 7 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/07/)

Up, and by water to [the Exchequer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/242/), where I got my [tallys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8499/) finished for the last quarter for [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/), and having paid all my fees I to [the Swan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1707/), whither I sent for some [oysters](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/373/), and thither comes [Mr. Falconbridge](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3671/) and [Spicer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1078/) and many more clerks; and there we eat and drank, and a great deal of their sorry discourse, and so parted, and I by coach [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), meeting [Balty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/631/) in the streete about [Charing Crosse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/138/) walking, which I am glad to see and spoke to him about his mustering business, I being now to give an account how the several muster-masters have behaved themselves, and so home to dinner, where finding the cloth laid and much crumpled but clean, I grew angry and flung the [trenchers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1779/) about the room, and in a mighty heat I was: so a clean cloth was laid, and my poor [wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) very patient, and so to dinner, and in comes [Mrs. Barbara Sheldon](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8955/), now Mrs. Wood, and dined with us, she mighty fine, and lives, I perceive, mighty happily, which I am glad [of] for her sake, but hate [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10246/) for a block-head in his choice. So away after dinner, leaving my wife and her, and by water to [the Strand](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/245/), and so to [the King’s playhouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/475/), where two acts were almost done when I come in; and there I sat with my cloak about my face, and saw the remainder of [“The Mayd’s Tragedy;”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10618/) a good play, and well acted, especially by the younger [Marshall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8437/), who is become a pretty good actor, and is the first play I have seen in either of the houses since before the great [plague](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/301/), they having acted now about fourteen days publickly. But I was in mighty pain lest I should be seen by any body to be at a play. Soon as done I home, and then to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) awhile, and then home and spent the night evening my [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) accounts, much to my satisfaction, and then to supper, and mighty good friends with my poor wife, and so to bed.

# [Saturday 8 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/08/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning, and at noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and there find [Mr. Pierce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/173/) and [his wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/785/) and [Betty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9044/), a pretty girle, who in discourse at table told me the great Proviso passed the [House of Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) yesterday; which makes [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) and Court mad, the King having given order to my [Lord Chamberlain](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/671/) to send to the playhouses and bawdy houses, to bid all the Parliament-men that were there to go to the Parliament presently. This is true, it seems; but it was carried against the Court by thirty or forty voices. It is a Proviso to the [Poll Bill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10745/), that there shall be a Committee of nine persons that shall have the inspection upon oath, and power of giving others, of all the accounts of the money given and spent for this warr. This hath a most sad face, and will breed very ill blood. He tells me, brought in by [Sir Robert Howard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10619/), who is one of the King’s servants, at least hath a great office, and hath got, they say, 20,000 _l._ since the King come in.

Mr. Pierce did also tell me as a great truth, as being told it by [Mr. Cowly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3530/), who was by, and heard it, that [Tom Killigrew](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/849/) should publiquely tell the King that his matters were coming into a very ill state; but that yet there was a way to help all, which is, says he, “There is a good, honest, able man, that I could name, that if your Majesty would employ, and command to see all things well executed, all things would soon be mended; and this is one Charles Stuart, who now spends his time in employing his lips … [and his prick – L&M] about the Court, and hath no other employment; but if you would give him this employment, he were the fittest man in the world to perform it.” This, he says, is most true.

But the King do not profit by any of this, but lays all aside, and remembers nothing, but to his pleasures again; which is a sorrowful consideration.

Very good company we were at dinner, and merry, and after dinner, he being gone about business, my wife and I and Mrs. Pierce and Betty and [Balty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/631/), who come to see us to-day very sick, and went home not well, together out, and our coach broke the wheel off upon [Ludgate Hill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/278/). So we were fain to part ourselves and get room in other people’s coaches, and Mrs. Pierce and I in one, and I carried her home and set her down, and myself to the [King’s playhouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/475/), which troubles me since, and hath cost me a forfeit of 10 _s._, which I have paid, and there did see a good part of [“The English Monsieur,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10620/) which is a mighty pretty play, very witty and pleasant. And the women do very well; but, above all, little [Nelly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5037/); that I am mightily pleased with the play, and much with the House, more than ever I expected, the women doing better than ever I expected, and very fine women.

Here I was in pain to be seen, and hid myself; but, as God would have it, [Sir John Chichly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10621/) come, and sat just by me.

Thence to Mrs. Pierce’s, and there took up my wife and away home, and to the office and [Sir W. Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/), of whom I hear that this Proviso in Parliament is mightily ill taken by all the Court party as a mortal blow, and that, that strikes deep into the [King’s prerogative](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/494/), which troubles me mightily.

Home, and set some papers right in my chamber, and then to supper and to bed, we being in much fear of ill news of our colliers. A fleete of two hundred sail, and fourteen Dutch men-of-war between them and us and they coming home with small convoy; and [the City](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/275/) in great want, coals being at 3 _l._ 3 _s._ per [chaldron](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7747/), as I am told. I saw smoke in the ruines this very day.

# [Sunday 9 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/09/)

(Lord’s day). Up, not to church, but to my chamber, and there begun to enter into this book my journall of September, which in the [fire](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10319/)-time I could not enter here, but in loose papers. At noon dined, and then to my chamber all the afternoon and night, looking over and tearing and burning all the unnecessary letters, which I have had upon my file for four or five years backward, which I intend to do quite through all my papers, that I may have nothing by me but what is worth keeping, and fit to be seen, if I should miscarry. At this work till midnight, and then to supper and to bed.

# [Monday 10 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/10/)

Up, and at [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) all the morning, and several people with me, [Sir W. Warren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/), who I do every day more and more admire for a miracle of cunning and forecast in his business, and then [Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), with whom I walked in the garden, and he tells me how angry the Court is at the late Proviso brought in by [the House](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/292/). How still my [Lord Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/) is, not daring to do or say any thing to displease the [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/); that the Parliament is in a very ill humour, and grows every day more and more so; and that the unskilfulness of the Court, and their difference among one another, is the occasion of all not agreeing in what they would have, and so they give leisure and occasion to the other part to run away with what the Court would not have.

Then comes [Mr. Gawden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/994/), and he and I in my chamber discoursing about his business, and to pay him some [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) orders which he delayed to receive till I had money instead of [tallies](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8499/), but do promise me consideration for my [victualling](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9960/) business for this year, and also as [Treasurer for Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8408/), which I am glad of, but would have been gladder to have just now received it. He gone, I alone to dinner at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and her people being gone down [the river](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1832/) to-day for pleasure, though a cold day and dark night to come up.

In the afternoon I to the [Excise Office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/291/) to enter my tallies, which I did, and come presently back again, and then to the office and did much business, and then home to supper, my wife and people being come well and hungry home from [Erith](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2697/). Then I to begin the setting of a Base to [“It is Decreed,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10288/) and so to bed.

# [Tuesday 11 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/11/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat, and at noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, a small dinner because of a good supper. After dinner [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I by coach to [St. Clement’s Church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/190/), to [Mrs. Turner’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/121/) lodgings, hard by, to take our leaves of her. She is returning into the North to her children, where, I perceive, [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1858/) hath clearly got the mastery of her, and she is likely to spend her days there, which for her sake I am a little sorry for, though for his it is but fit she should live where he hath a mind. Here were several people come to see and take leave of her, she going to-morrow: among others, my [Lady Mordant](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10634/), which was Betty Turner, a most homely widow, but young, and pretty rich, and good natured. Thence, having promised to write every month to her, we home, and I to my office, while my wife to get things together for supper. Dispatching my business at the office. Anon come our guests, old [Mr. Batelier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10243/), and [his son](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10208/) and daughter, [Mercer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7761/), which was all our company. We had a good [venison pasty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/384/) and other good cheer, and as merry as in so good, innocent, and understanding company I could be. He is much troubled that [wines](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/), laden by him in France before the late proclamation was out, cannot now be brought into England, which is so much to his and other merchants’ loss.

We sat long at supper and then to talk, and so late parted and so to bed. This day the [Poll Bill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10745/) was to be passed, and great endeavours used to take away the Proviso.

# [Wednesday 12 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/12/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where some accounts of [Mr. Gawden’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/994/) were examined, but I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) most of the morning to even some accounts with [Sir H. Cholmly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5179/), [Mr. Moone](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9606/), and others one after another. Sir H. Cholmly did with grief tell me how the [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) hath been told plainly that [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) hath been heard to say, that he would dissolve them rather than pass this Bill with the Proviso; but tells me, that the Proviso is removed, and now carried that it shall be done by a Bill by itself. He tells me how the King hath lately paid about 30,000 _l._1 to clear debts of my [Lady Castlemayne’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1062/); and that she and [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3375/) are parted for ever, upon good terms, never to trouble one another more. He says that he hears 400,000 _l._ hath gone into the Privypurse since this warr; and that that hath consumed so much of our money, and makes the King and Court so mad to be brought to discover it.

He gone, and after him the rest, I to the office, and at noon to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), where the very good newes is just come of our four ships from [Smyrna](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10591/), come safe without convoy even into [the Downes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1257/), without seeing any enemy; which is the best, and indeed only considerable good newes to our Exchange, since the burning of [the City](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/275/); and it is strange to see how it do cheer up men’s hearts. Here I saw shops now come to be in this Exchange, and met little [Batelier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10208/), who sits here but at 3 _l._ per annum, whereas he sat at the other at 100 _l._, which he says he believes will prove of as good account to him now as the other did at that rent. From the ’Change to [Captain Cocke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), and there, by agreement, dined, and there was [Charles Porter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5703/), [Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9022/), [Fern](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1637/), [Debasty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8957/), whose bad English and pleasant discourses was exceeding good entertainment, [Matt. Wren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8019/), [Major Cooper](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9751/), and myself, mighty merry and pretty discourse.

They talked for certain, that now the King do follow [Mrs. Stewart](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5036/) wholly, and my Lady Castlemayne not above once a week; that the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) do not haunt my [Lady Denham](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10044/) so much; that she troubles him with matters of State, being of my [Lord Bristoll’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2845/) faction, and that he avoids; that she is ill still.

After dinner I away to the office, where we sat late upon [Mr. Gawden’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/994/) accounts, [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) being gone home sick. I late at the office, and then home to supper and to bed, being mightily troubled with a pain in the small of my back, through cold, or (which I think most true) my straining last night to get open my [plate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7982/) chest, in such pain all night I could not turn myself in my bed. Newes this day from [Brampton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1768/), of [Mr. Ensum](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9784/), [my sister’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1568/) sweetheart, being dead: a clowne.

1.
